Weak Hopf symmetry and tube algebra of the generalized multifusion string-net model
Zhian Jia, Sheng Tan, Dagomir Kaszlikowski

Abstract
We investigate the multifusion generalization of string-net ground states and lattice Hamiltonians, delving into its associated weak Hopf symmetry. For the multifusion string-net, the gauge symmetry manifests as a general weak Hopf algebra, leading to a reducible vacuum string label; the charge symmetry, serving as a quantum double of gauge symmetry, constitutes a connected weak Hopf algebra. This implies that the associated topological phase retains its characterization by a unitary modular tensor category (UMTC). The bulk charge symmetry can also be captured by a weak Hopf tube algebra. We offer an explicit construction of the weak Hopf tube algebra structure and thoroughly discuss its properties. The gapped boundary and domain wall models are extensively discussed, with these 1 ​ d 1d phases characterized by unitary multifusion categories (UMFCs). We delve into the gauge and charge symmetries of these 1 ​ d 1d phases, as well as the construction of the boundary and domain wall tube algebras. Additionally, we illustrate that the domain wall tube algebra can be regarded as a cross product of two boundary tube algebras. As an application of our model, we elucidate how to interpret the defective string-net as a restricted multifusion string-net.



1
Introduction

Exotic quantum phases of matter have attracted substantial attention in recent decades
Sachdev 2011
;
Wen 2004
;
Zeng et al. 2019
;
Simon 2023
. Apart from their fundamental significance, these phases hold potential applications in quantum information and computation tasks, such as the development of robust topological quantum error-correction codes (QECC)
Dennis et al. 2002
;
Terhal 2015
and topological quantum computation (TQC)
Kitaev 2003
;
Freedman et al. 2002
;
Nayak et al. 2008
;
Wang 2010
;
Pachos 2012
.
There are roughly three types of quantum phases at zero temperature
Chatterjee et al. 2023
;
Wen 2023
: (i) Gapped phase, characterized by the absence of low-energy excitations, with all excitations exhibiting an energy gap; (ii) Gapless phase with finite low-energy modes, exemplified by Dirac or Weyl semimetals, superfluids, etc.; (iii) Gapless phase with infinite low-energy modes, as observed in Fermi metals, Bose metals, etc.
In this work, we will focus on the gapped phase.

In a gapped quantum phase, there exist two types of excitations: local excitations, which can be created or annihilated by local operators, and topological excitations, which cannot. A gapped phase featuring topological excitations is termed a topologically ordered phase.
The universal low-energy and long-distance properties of gapped phases of quantum matter are described by topological quantum field theory (TQFT)
Witten 1988
;
Dijkgraaf and Witten 1990
;
Wen 2004
;
Wang 2010
;
Pachos 2012
;
Simon 2023
;
Zeng et al. 2019
.
Topological phases display unique attributes like long-range entanglement
Zeng et al. 2019
, fractional statistics
Wilczek 1990
, and topologically protected ground state degeneracy
Wen 1989
;
Wen and Niu 1990
;
Kitaev 2003
;
Levin and Wen 2005
. These characteristics distinguish them from conventional models, notably deviating from Landau’s spontaneous symmetry breaking framework
Landau 1937
.

Topologically ordered phases are termed anomaly-free if they can be realized by a local lattice Hamiltonian in the same dimension
Kong and Wen 2014
;
Wen 2013
. Otherwise, they are referred to as anomalous.
In the context of
2d
fusion topologically ordered phases
1
1

1

Here by fusion we mean the vacuum sector of the topological phase is simple.
, it is well known that they are classified, up to
E_{8}
quantum Hall states, by the unitary modular tensor categories (UMTCs) representing the topological excitations in the bulk
Kitaev 2006
.
The topological excitations in the bulk are point-like quasi-particles that cannot be created or annihilated by local operators from the vacuum sector or its direct sums. They exhibit fusion, splitting into a direct sum of other topological excitations, and braiding interactions among each other.
The vacuum sector
\mathbf{1}
is the tensor unit of the UMTC
\mathcal{B}
.
The
2d
fusion topologically ordered phases can also be classified into two families depending on its chiral central charge
c=c_{R}-c_{L}

Kane and Fisher 1997
: (i) chiral
c\neq 0
, where time-reversal symmetry is broken, and (ii) non-chiral
c=0
, where time-reversal symmetry is preserved.
In the UMTC framework, a non-chiral UMTC denoted as
\mathcal{B}
is defined such that there exists a unitary multifusion category (UMFC)
\mathcal{D}
where
\mathcal{B}
is braided monoidal equivalent to the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
.

Turaev and Viro introduced a state-sum invariant for 3-manifolds rooted in a ribbon fusion category
Turaev and Viro 1992
. This framework was later broadened by Barrett and Westbury to encompass the spherical fusion category
Barrett and Westbury 1996
.
The Levin-Wen string-net model
2
2

2

Throughout this work, when referring to the “Levin-Wen string-net model”, we specifically mean the string-net model with input data being a unitary fusion category (UFC).
provides a lattice interpretation of the Turaev-Viro-Barrett-Westbury TQFT
Levin and Wen 2005
;
Kirillov Jr 2011
;
Lan and Wen 2014
;
Lin and Levin 2014
;
Lin et al. 2021
;
Hahn and Wolf 2020
and a construction of the explicit Hamiltonian.
The Levin-Wen string-net model is a lattice realization of non-chiral topologically ordered phases.
Kitaev quantum double model is also a crucial lattice model for non-chiral topological phases, which can be regarded as a lattice gauge theory
Kitaev 2003
. It has been established that for a
C^{*}
Hopf algebra
H
, the Kitaev quantum double model is equivalent to the Levin-Wen string-net model with input UFC
\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{Rep}(H)

Buerschaper and Aguado 2009
;
Buerschaper et al. 2013a
;
Buerschaper et al. 2013b
;
Jia et al. 2023a
.
However, it is established that not all UFCs can be represented as the representation category of a Hopf algebra. Thus, we need to consider more general quantum symmetries, and it turns out the symmetries are characterized by weak Hopf algebras
Böhm et al. 1999
.
The quantum symmetry behind a general Levin-Wen string-net model is a weak Hopf algebra in the sense that every UFC can be expressed as a representation category for some weak Hopf algebra
Szlachányi 2001
;
Ostrik 2003
.
The lattice gauge theory with gauge symmetry characterized by a weak Hopf algebra is established in Refs.
Jia et al. 2023b
;
Chang 2014
. This prompts the question: what is the general string-net realization of a topological phase with general weak Hopf symmetry? The answer lies in the multifusion string-net model. This is because the representation category of a weak Hopf algebra is generally not a fusion category but a multifusion category.

In this work, our primary focus is on the multifusion generalization of the Levin-Wen string-net model, exploring both the macroscopic (algebraic) theory and the microscopic lattice Hamiltonian realization.
We will use the correspondence between the multifusion string-net and the weak Hopf lattice gauge theory to study the bulk topological phases, gapped boundary theory and gapped domain wall theory.
The connection and difference between the multifusion string-net and the Levin-Wen string-net will be stressed.

To characterize the topological excitations, we introduce a weak Hopf tube algebra. It is worth noting that the investigation of tube algebras has a long history since Ocneanu’s original works
Ocneanu 1994
;
Ocneanu 2001
.
A key property of the tube algebra is that its representation category is equivalent to the category of topological excitations of the model
Ocneanu 1994
;
Ocneanu 2001
;
Simon 2023
;
Izumi 2000
;
Izumi 2001
;
Müger 2003
;
Christian et al. 2023
;
Kawagoe et al. 2024
. Previous formulations of tube algebras lack a coalgebra structure and therefore do not qualify as weak Hopf algebras. In line with this principle, we use the term “tube algebra” to denote the local algebra for which the representation category coincides with the topological phase.
For the boundary of the Levin-Wen model, a weak Hopf local algebra is proposed in Ref.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
, where the authors utilize topological local moves to derive the simplest configuration of a boundary tube region and construct the weak Hopf structure for this region.
However, for the bulk, performing topological local moves to obtain the simplest configuration results in a Q-algebra
Lan and Wen 2014
, which lacks a coalgebra structure.
Our observation suggests that we should treat the bulk excitation as a domain wall defect. By doing so, when performing the topological local moves, we can obtain a tube region with a symmetric structure, enabling us to equip it with a weak Hopf algebra structure.

The gapped boundary and domain wall theory for Levin-Wen string-net model (and Kitaev quantum double model) have been extensively investigated in Refs.
Bravyi and Kitaev 1998
;
Bombin and Martin-Delgado 2008
;
Freedman and Meyer 2001
;
Beigi et al. 2011
;
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Levin 2013
;
Levin 2013
;
Wang and Wen 2015
;
Cong et al. 2017
;
Wang et al. 2020
;
Jia et al. 2023a
;
Jia et al. 2023b
.
For the multifusion string-net model, we also explore the gapped boundary and gapped domain wall theories from the perspective of weak Hopf symmetry. The weak Hopf tube algebras for the boundary and domain wall are also constructed.
A crucial observation is that the
1d
phases for the multifusion string-net model are generally not UFCs, but rather UMFCs.
We develop the anyon condensation theory for these scenarios, where the condensation is generally characterized by a pair of algebras in the bulk phase: one condensable algebra and another algebra over this condensable algebra.

As an application of our model, we also demonstrate how to interpret a defective Levin-Wen string-net as a special case of the multifusion string-net following the discussion outlined in Ref.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
.

This paper is organized as follows:

In Sec.
2
, we delve into the macroscopic (algebraic) theory of the multifusion string-net. We emphasize the weak Hopf symmetry underlying the model and provide a review of the necessary preliminaries of concepts about multifusion categories and weak Hopf algebras in this section.
We introduce the weak Hopf gauge symmetry for the multifusion string-net, based on the fact that a multifusion string-net is equivalent to a weak Hopf lattice gauge theory.
We also introduce the weak Hopf charge symmetry, for which the topological charges are irreducible representations of this weak Hopf algebra. As will be discussed in Sec.
4
, we construct the explicit weak Hopf tube algebra, which can be regarded as the charge symmetry of the multifusion string-net.
The boundary tube algebra constructed in Sec.
5
can be regarded as a gauge symmetry of the bulk via the bulk-boundary duality.

In Sec.
3
, we give a detailed construction of the multifusion string-net ground state and the lattice Hamiltonian. We show that this lattice Hamiltonian is a local commutative projector (LCP) Hamiltonian and some properties of the Hamiltonian are discussed in detail.

In Sec.
4
, we develop the theory of the bulk tube algebra. By treating the bulk excitations as defects on domain walls and performing the topological local moves, we derive a tube algebra. We then construct a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra structure for this tube algebra. The bulk topological excitations are represented by the tube algebra, and we also explore the Morita theory of the tube algebra.

Sec.
5
and Sec.
6
focus on the gapped boundary and domain wall theories of the multifusion string-net. We demonstrate that these
1d
phases are characterized by UMFCs. The gauge symmetry and charge symmetry for these phases are thoroughly discussed. Furthermore, we construct the boundary and domain wall tube algebras, which can be interpreted as the charge symmetries of the corresponding phases. Additionally, we illustrate how to derive the
1d
UMFC topological phase from the bulk UMFC phases by establishing the corresponding anyon condensation theory.

In the last part, we present an application of the multifusion string-net model, demonstrating how to interpret the defective Levin-Wen string-net as a restricted multifusion string-net. In Sec.
8
, we offer concluding remarks and discuss potential future directions and questions.

2
Macroscopic theory of multifusion string-net and weak Hopf symmetry

In Landau’s symmetry-breaking theory
Landau 1937
, symmetries are described by groups. Consider a quantum system
(H,\mathcal{V}_{GS})
, where
H
is the Hamiltonian and
\mathcal{V}_{GS}
is the ground state subspace. A Hamiltonian symmetry
G_{H}
is a group for which there exists a unitary or antiunitary representation
g\mapsto U_{g}
such that
[U_{g},H]=0
for all
g\in G_{H}
.
The ground state symmetry
G_{GS}
is a group such that
U_{g}
stabilizes
\mathcal{V}_{GS}
for all
g\in G_{GS}
.
It is clear that
G_{H}\subset G_{GS}
.
The topologically ordered phase is beyond the Landau’s symmetry breaking paradigm, as their symmetries are described by quantum groups
Bais et al. 2003
;
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Buerschaper et al. 2013a
;
Meusburger 2017
;
Jia et al. 2023a
;
Jia et al. 2023b
;
Szlachányi 2023
or fusion categories
Levin and Wen 2005
;
Lan and Wen 2014
;
Lin and Levin 2014
;
Lin et al. 2021
.

The original Levin-Wen string-net model is constructed from a UFC
\mathcal{C}
, where the topological excitations are described by the UMTC
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})
, which is the Drinfeld center of
\mathcal{C}
. It is natural to inquire about the quantum symmetry of the string-net model. The answer to this question is that its symmetry is characterized by a weak Hopf algebra
W
.
For any UFC
\mathcal{C}
we can find a
connected weak Hopf algebra
such that
\mathcal{C}
is equivalent to the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
of
W
as fusion category
Ostrik 2003
.
This enables us to establish an equivalence between the string-net model and lattice gauge theory with gauge symmetry described by a weak Hopf algebra, which has been recently constructed as a generalization of the Kitaev quantum double model
Chang 2014
;
Jia et al. 2023b
.
It is worthy to mentioning that Hopf algebra lattice gauge theory
Buerschaper et al. 2013a
;
Meusburger 2017
;
Jia et al. 2023a
is not enough to describe this equivalence, since there exist some examples of monoidal categories that cannot be regarded as the representation category of Hopf algebras
Ostrik 2003
.
This implies that we need to consider weak Hopf lattice gauge theory. Consequently, a natural question arises: what is the string-net model corresponding to a general weak Hopf lattice gauge theory? The answer is the multifusion string-net model, which will be elaborated later in this work.
To summarize, we have a correspondence as shown in Table

2.1
Unitary multifusion category

Let us first recall some basic definitions and results about the multifusion category.
See Refs.
Etingof et al. 2016
;
Turaev 2016
;
Turaev and Virelizier 2017
for more details.
The reader familiar with the notion of the multifusion category might skip this part and get back if necessary.

•

A
\mathbb{C}
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
is a category where all Hom spaces are finite-dimensional vector spaces and the compositions of morphisms are linear maps with respect to each component. An object
X\in\mathcal{C}
is called simple if
\operatorname{End}(X)\cong\mathbb{C}\mathrm{id}_{X}
.

\mathcal{C}
is called finite if there is only a finite number of inequivalent simple objects in
\mathcal{C}
; we usually denote the set of equivalence classes of simple objects of
\mathcal{C}
as
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{C})
.
\mathcal{C}
is called semisimple if every object in
\mathcal{C}
is a direct sum of simple objects.

•

A monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is a category equipped with a tensor product
\otimes:\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
and a tensor unit
\mathbf{1}
. The tensor product is associative with the associativity isomorphisms
a_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)
, which are required to obey the pentagon relation. The left and right unit isomorphisms
l_{X}:\mathbf{1}\otimes X\to X
and
r_{X}:X\otimes\mathbf{1}\to X
are required to obey the triangle relation.
A monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is called
\mathbb{C}
-linear if
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathbb{C}
-linear and the tensor product of morphisms is
\mathbb{C}
-linear with respect to each component. In our context, a monoidal category that is
\mathbb{C}
-linear will be referred to as a tensor category.

•

A monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is called rigid if each object
X
has a left dual
{{}^{\vee}}\!X
and a right dual
X^{\vee}
together with the duality maps

3

3

d_{X}
primarily represents the quantum dimension of an object. However, in this particular context, we employ it to symbolize the “death” map. This dual usage should not lead to confusion given the distinct scenarios where each is applied.

\displaystyle\text{left:}\quad b_{X}:\mathbf{1}\to X\otimes X^{\vee},\quad d_{X}:X^{\vee}\otimes X\to\mathbf{1},

(1)

\displaystyle\text{right:}\quad b^{\prime}_{X}:\mathbf{1}\to{{}^{\vee}}\!X\otimes X,\quad d^{\prime}_{X}:X\otimes{{}^{\vee}}\!X\to\mathbf{1},

(2)

which satisfy the following conditions:

(4)

\mathcal{C}
is called sovereign if
{{}^{\vee}}\!X\cong X^{\vee}
for all
X\in\mathcal{C}
.

•

A
\dagger
-category is a
\mathbb{C}
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
equipped with an involutive antilinear contravariant functor
\dagger:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
which acts trivially on objects
X^{\dagger}=X
for all
X\in\mathcal{C}
. When acting on Hom spaces, it satisfies
(i)
f^{\dagger}\in\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)
if
f\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
and
f^{\dagger\dagger}=f
for all
f\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
;
(ii)
(c_{1}f_{1}+c_{2}f_{2})^{\dagger}=\bar{c}_{1}f_{1}^{\dagger}+\bar{c}_{2}f_{2}^{\dagger}
for all
c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{C}
and
f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
;
(iii)
{\mathrm{id}}_{X}^{\dagger}=\mathrm{id}_{X}
for all
X\in\mathcal{C}

4
4

4

This condition can be inferred from the others:
\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}^{\dagger\dagger}=(\mathrm{id}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\mathrm{id}^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=\mathrm{id}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\mathrm{id}^{\dagger}=\mathrm{id}^{\dagger}
.
But for clarity, we have explicitly stated it.
; (iv)
(f\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}g)^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}f^{\dagger}
for all morphisms
f\in\mathrm{Hom}(Y,Z),g\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
.
A
\dagger
-category
\mathcal{C}
is called unitary if
f^{\dagger}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}f=0
implies
f=0
.

•

A monoidal
\dagger
-category
\mathcal{C}
is a category that possesses both a monoidal and a
\dagger
-category structures. It ensures:
(i) For all
f\in\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
and
g\in\mathrm{Hom}(Z,W)
,
(f\otimes g)^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}\otimes g^{\dagger}
;
(ii) The associativity isomorphisms uphold
a_{X,Y,Z}^{\dagger}=a^{-1}_{X,Y,Z}
, while the left and right isomorphisms abide by
l_{X}^{\dagger}=l_{X}^{-1}
and
r_{X}^{\dagger}=r_{X}^{-1}
respectively.

•

A pivotal structure on a rigid monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
is a natural isomorphism
p:\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\to(\cdot)^{\vee\vee}
which satisfies
p_{X\otimes Y}\cong p_{X}\otimes p_{Y}
for all
X,Y\in\mathcal{C}
(here “
\cong
” means that they are equal up to some canonical isomorphisms).
A pivotal category is a rigid monoidal category with a given pivotal structure.
Via pivotal structure
\{p_{X}\}
, we can define left and right traces of a morphism
f\in\operatorname{End}(X)
as (we omit the isomorphism
\mathbf{1}^{\vee}\cong\mathbf{1}
)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}^{L}(f)=b_{X^{\vee}}^{\vee}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\gamma_{X^{\vee\vee}\otimes X^{\vee}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(p_{X^{\vee}}\otimes p_{X})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mathrm{id}_{X^{\vee}}\otimes f)\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mathrm{id}_{X^{\vee}}\otimes p_{X}^{-1})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}b_{X^{\vee}},

(5)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}^{R}(f)=b_{X^{\vee}}^{\vee}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\gamma_{X\otimes X^{\vee}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(p_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X^{\vee}})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X^{\vee}})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}b_{X},

(6)

where

are natural transformations induced by the rigidity structure. Notice that both
\operatorname{Tr}^{L}(f),\operatorname{Tr}^{R}(f)\in\operatorname{End}(\mathbf{1})
.
A spherical category is a pivotal category for which
\operatorname{Tr}^{L}(f)=\operatorname{Tr}^{R}(f)
for all morphisms

.

5

5

In the context of multifusion categories, the concept of “spherical” can be directly extended. The essential requirement is the equality of the left and right traces as complex numbers. Notably, given that the left and right traces are morphisms in distinct components, a more in-depth analysis can be found in Refs.

;

In a monoidal
\dagger
-category, given an object

with a right dual
(X^{\vee},b_{X},d_{X})

(X^{\vee},d_{X}^{\dagger},b_{X}^{\dagger})

\bar{X}=X^{*}:=X^{\vee}={{}^{\vee}}X
.

For a monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
, we define
\mathcal{C}^{\rm rev}
such that
X\otimes^{\rm rev}Y:=Y\otimes X
. For a braided category
\mathcal{C}
,

Definition 1
.

A multifusion category over
\mathbb{C}
is a finite semisimple
\mathbb{C}
-linear rigid monoidal category.
A fusion category is a multifusion category whose tensor unit is simple.

When
\mathcal{D}
is a multifusion category, since
\mathbf{1}
may not be simple, it can be decomposed as
\mathbf{1}=\oplus_{i\in I}\mathbf{1}_{i}
with
\mathbf{1}_{i}
simple for all
i\in I
.
It can be proved that
\mathbf{1}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{j}\cong\delta_{i,j}\mathbf{1}_{i}
and each
\mathbf{1}_{i}
has left and right duals such that
\mathbf{1}_{i}^{\vee}\cong\mathbf{1}_{i}\cong{{}^{\vee}}\mathbf{1}_{i}
.
Let
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}:=\mathbf{1}_{i}\otimes\mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{j}
, then we have a decomposition (as additive category)

\mathcal{D}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j},

(7)

which will be referred to as the canonical grading of
\mathcal{D}
.
Every simple object in
\mathcal{D}
belongs to some
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
.
The tensor product maps
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}\times\mathcal{D}_{k,l}
to zero when
j\neq k
and to
\mathcal{D}_{i,l}
when
j=k
.
The categories
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
are fusion categories with the tensor unit
\mathbf{1}_{i}
.
If
X\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
has left or right dual, then this dual must be in
\mathcal{D}_{j,i}
.

It has been demonstrated in Refs.
Reutter 2023
;
Ciamprone et al. 2023
that the unitary structure of every
C^{*}
fusion category, if it exists, must be unique (up to natural isomorphisms). However, for
C^{*}
multifusion categories, there may exist inequivalent unitary structures on them.

Example 1

(UMFC
\mathsf{Mat}_{n}
)
.

A typical example of UMFC is the one constructed from
n\times n
matrices
\mathsf{Mat}_{n}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathsf{M}_{i,j}
. The index set
I=\{1,\cdots,n\}
, and each component
\mathsf{M}_{i,j}
contains exactly one simple object
\mathds{I}_{i,j}
which can be regarded as the matrix basis
\mathds{I}_{i,j}=|i\rangle\langle j|
.
The tensor product obeys the matrix multiplication rule
\mathds{I}_{i,j}\otimes\mathds{I}_{k,l}=\delta_{j,k}\mathds{I}_{i,l}
.
Each diagonal component
\mathsf{M}_{i,i}
is a UFC equivalent to
\mathsf{Vect}
, the category of all finite-dimensional vector spaces.
The rigidity is given by
\mathds{I}_{i,j}^{*}=\mathds{I}_{j,i}
, and all structural isomorphisms are the identity map.

Drinfeld center of multifusion category.
—
The Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
of a multifusion category
\mathcal{D}
is defined as follows. The objects of
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
are pairs
(X,c_{X,\bullet})
with
c_{X,\bullet}=\{c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\xrightarrow{\sim}Y\otimes X\}_{Y\in\mathcal{D}}
called half-braiding.
A morphism
f
between
(X,c_{X,\bullet})
and
(Y,c_{Y,\bullet})
is a morphism
f:X\to Y
such that
(\mathrm{id}_{Z}\otimes f)\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}c_{X,Z}=c_{Y,Z}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_{Z})
. The Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
is a braided category. It is well known that the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
is equivalent to the
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
as braided monoidal categories
Kong and Zheng 2018
.
If
\mathcal{D}
is rigid, then
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
is also rigid. Similarly, if
\mathcal{D}
is pivotal, then
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
is also pivotal. Moreover, the following result holds:

Lemma 1
.

For an indecomposable multifusion category
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
, we have

1.

The Drinfeld center of the diagonal component
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
are braided monoidal equivalent,
viz.
,
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i,i})\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{j,j})
for all
i,j\in I
.

2.

The Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
of
\mathcal{D}
is braided monoidal equivalent to
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i,i})
for all
i\in I
.

Proof.

The proofs of statements 1 and 2 can be found in Refs.
(
Chang et al. 2015
, Theorem 2.4)
and
(
Kong and Zheng 2018
, Theorem 2.5.1)
, respectively.
∎

Notice that the non-chiral topological phase is usually defined as a UMTC
\mathcal{B}
for which there exists a UFC
\mathcal{C}
such that
\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})
as braided monoidal categories. From the above result and the fact that any UFC can be embedded into a UMFC (see Sec.
7
), we see that the non-chiral topological phase
\mathcal{B}
can be equivalently defined as a UMTC
\mathcal{B}
for which there exists a UMFC
\mathcal{D}
such that
\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
as braided monoidal categories.

For a UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, given that
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
are all UFCs, their Drinfeld centers
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i,i})
are UMTCs. A direct consequence of statement 2 in the lemma above is that the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
of an indecomposable UMFC
\mathcal{D}
is a UMTC.
As we delve further into our exploration, it becomes evident that the above result guarantees the utility of any given UMFC in constructing defective string-net models characterized by gapped boundaries, boundary defects, and other features.

2.2
Weak Hopf symmetry for
2d
topological phase

The group symmetry of a quantum system can be regarded as a group action on the system’s Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
, i.e., for each
g\in G
, we have
U_{g}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
satisfying
U_{gh}=U_{g}U_{h}
and
U_{e}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{H}}
.
Consider the group algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]
, the Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
is a
\mathbb{C}[G]
-module.
The ground state
\Psi\in\mathcal{H}
is invariant under the
\mathbb{C}[G]
-action in the sense that

(\sum_{g\in G}c_{g}g)\triangleright\Psi=\sum_{g\in G}c_{g}\Psi=\varepsilon(\sum_{g\in G}c_{g}g)\Psi,

(8)

where
\varepsilon:\mathbb{C}[G]\to\mathbb{C}
is the counit map of the group algebra.
This motivates the introduction of Hopf algebra symmetry, defined as
h\triangleright\Psi=\varepsilon(h)\Psi

Bais et al. 2003
. However, this definition cannot be straightforwardly extended to the weak Hopf case, as the trivial representation exhibits a nontrivial algebra action. To address this challenge, in Ref.
Jia et al. 2023b
, we introduce the concept of weak Hopf symmetry.
The weak Hopf symmetry plays a pivotal role in comprehending the string-net model. In the following, we will recall the definition of weak Hopf symmetry and discuss its properties.

Let us first introduce the weak Hopf algebra within the braided multifusion category. In this work, our primary focus will be on the case of the category of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, denoted as
\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}
. A
weak bialgebra

(W,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon)
is an object
W\in\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}
equipped with the following structure morphisms (here
\mathbf{1}=\mathbb{C}
):

(17)

A
weak Hopf algebra

(W,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)
is a weak bialgebra
(W,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon)
equipped with a morphism
S:W\to W
called antipode which satisfies the following three conditions:

(1)

(20)

A complex weak Hopf algebra
W
is termed simple if its underlying algebra
(W,\mu,\eta)
possesses no nontrivial subalgebras. It is referred to as semisimple if its underlying algebra can be expressed as a direct sum of simple algebras.

A useful tool for investigating the weak Hopf algebra is the canonical pairing between
W
and its dual
\hat{W}:=\mathrm{Hom}(W,\mathbb{C})
. For
\phi\in\hat{W}
and
x\in W
, we define
\langle\phi,x\rangle:=\phi(x)
.

\hat{W}
has a canonical weak Hopf algebra structure with structure maps given by:

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\mu}(\varphi\otimes\psi),x\rangle=\langle\varphi\otimes\psi,\Delta(x)\rangle,

(21)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\eta}(1),x\rangle=\varepsilon(x),\,\text{i.e.,}\hat{1}=\varepsilon,

(22)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\Delta}(\varphi),x\otimes y\rangle=\langle\varphi,\mu(x\otimes y)\rangle,

(23)

\displaystyle\hat{\varepsilon}(\varphi)=\langle\varphi,\eta(1)\rangle,

(24)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{S}(\varphi),x\rangle=\langle\varphi,S(x)\rangle.

(25)

The opposite weak Hopf algebra
W^{\rm op}
is defined as
(W,\mu^{\rm op},\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon,S^{-1})
, and the co-opposite weak Hopf algebra
W^{\rm cop}
is defined as
(W,\mu,\eta,\Delta^{\rm op},\varepsilon,S^{-1})
. Note that the antipode is always invertible
Böhm et al. 1999
.

Definition 2

(Quantum double, see Ref.
Jia et al. 2023b
for details)
.

For a weak Hopf algebra
W\in\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}
, its quantum double is defined as the space
D(W)=(\hat{W}\otimes W)/J
where
J
is generated by

\phi\otimes lh-\phi(l\rightharpoonup\varepsilon)\otimes h,\quad\phi\otimes rh-\phi(\varepsilon\leftharpoonup r)\otimes h,\quad l\in W_{L},\;r\in W_{R}.

(26)

D(W)
is equipped with the following weak Hopf algebra structure:

(1)

The multiplication
[\varphi\otimes h][\psi\otimes g]=\sum_{(\psi),(h)}[\varphi\psi^{(2)}\otimes h^{(2)}g]\langle\psi^{(1)},S^{-1}(h^{(3)})\rangle\langle\psi^{(3)},h^{(1)}\rangle
.

(2)

The unit
[\varepsilon\otimes 1_{W}]
.

(3)

The comultiplication
\Delta([\varphi\otimes h])=\sum_{(\varphi),(h)}[\varphi^{(2)}\otimes h^{(1)}]\otimes[\varphi^{(1)}\otimes h^{(2)}]
.

(4)

The counit
\varepsilon([\varphi\otimes h])=\langle\varphi,\varepsilon_{R}(S^{-1}(h))\rangle
.

(5)

The antipode
S([\varphi\otimes h])=\sum_{(\varphi),(h)}[\hat{S}^{-1}(\varphi^{(2)})\otimes S(h^{(2)})]\langle\varphi^{(1)},h^{(3)}\rangle\langle\varphi^{(3)},S^{-1}(h^{(1)})\rangle
.

The quantum double has a canonical quasitriangular structure, ensuring that the representation category of
D(W)
is braided. Notice that here and henceforth we adopt Sweedler’s notation for comultiplication
\Delta(x)=\sum_{(x)}x^{(1)}\otimes x^{(2)}
, and for arrows
(a\rightharpoonup\phi)(h)=\phi(ha)
,
(\phi\leftharpoonup a)(h)=\phi(ah)
.

Example 2
.

The following are some examples of weak Hopf algebras:

1.

For every Hopf algebra
H
, its dynamical twist is a weak Hopf algebra.

2.

If
B
is a separable algebra, then its enveloping algebra
B^{\rm op}\otimes B
can be equipped with a weak Hopf algebra structure
Nikshych et al. 2003
.

For a given weak Hopf symmetry
W
, the symmetry charges (or sectors) are defined as finite-dimensional irreducible representations of
W
(left
W
-modules, the action will be denoted as “
x\triangleright z
”).
The category of these symmetry charges is denoted as
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
, where the morphisms between two charges
X
and
Y
are
W
-linear homomorphisms.
The fusion between
X,Y\in\mathsf{Rep}(W)
are defined as

X\otimes Y:=\{x\in X\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}Y:\Delta(1)\triangleright x=x\}.

(27)

Since
\Delta(1)
is an idempotent, we see
X\otimes Y=\Delta(1)\triangleright(X\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}Y)
.
The vacuum charge is the left counital subalgebra
\mathbf{1}=W_{L}=\varepsilon_{L}(W)
with the left
W
-action given by
x\triangleright z=\varepsilon_{L}(xz)
.
For a charge
X
, its anti-charge is defined as
\bar{X}:=\mathrm{Hom}(X,\mathbb{C})
, with the left
W
action given by
(x\triangleright f)(y)=f(S(x)y)
for
f\in\bar{X}
.
The duality maps
b_{X}:\mathbf{1}\to X\otimes\bar{X}
and
d_{X}:\bar{X}\otimes X\to\mathbf{1}
are given by:
b_{X}(x)=x\,\triangleright\,(\sum_{i}v_{i}\otimes f_{i})
where
\{v_{i}\}
and
\{f_{i}\}

are bases of
X
and
\bar{X}
respectively which are dual to each other, and
d_{X}(\sum_{j}g_{j}\otimes z_{j})=\sum_{j}\sum_{(1)}g_{j}(1^{(1)}z_{j})1^{(2)}
where
\sum_{j}g_{j}\otimes z_{j}\in\bar{X}\otimes X
.
The weak Hopf algebra
W
is called
indecomposable
if and only if
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
is indecomposable as a tensor category.

Definition 3

(Weak Hopf symmetry)
.

For a quantum system
(H,\mathcal{H})
, we assert that it possesses a weak Hopf symmetry if
\mathcal{H}
forms a representation of
W
.
This implies that we can establish a mapping from
g\in W
to operators
U_{g}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
such that
U_{gh}=U_{g}U_{h}
and
U_{1}=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{H}}
. We will also denote the action simply as
g\triangleright\Psi
. A subspace
\mathcal{V}
of
\mathcal{H}
is called a vacuum space if and only if it is the ground state space of Hamiltonian
H
and is isomorphic to the direct sum of trivial representations of
W
.

Remark 2.1
.

In Ref.
Jia et al. 2023b
, we introduce the weak Hopf symmetry for a given state
\Psi\in\mathcal{H}
. Recall that
\mathcal{H}
is a
W
-module.
\Psi
is called invariant under the action of
g\in W
if
g\triangleright\Psi=\varepsilon_{L}(g)\triangleright\Psi
. This is a special case of the weak Hopf symmetry given above.

Lemma 2
.

For every multifusion category
\mathcal{C}
, there is a (non-unique) corresponding weak Hopf algebra
W
such that
\mathcal{C}
is equivalent to the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
as UMFCs.

Proof.

See Refs.
Szlachányi 2001
,
(
Ostrik 2003
, Theorem 4.1)
,
(
Etingof et al. 2005
, Corollary 2.22)
for a detailed discussion.
∎

Definition 4

(Connected weak Hopf algebra
Etingof et al. 2005
)
.

If the vacuum sector of a weak Hopf algebra
W
is irreducible, then
W
is called connected (or pure). In this case, the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
is a UFC.
The vacuum sector
W_{L}
is irreducible if and only if the intersection of
W_{L}
and the center
Z(W)
is
\mathbb{C}
.

Proposition 1
.

We have the following two crucial results about the quantum double of a weak Hopf symmetry:

1.

The quantum double
D(W)
of any indecomposable weak Hopf algebra
W
is a connected weak Hopf algebra.

2.

For every non-chiral topological phase (UMTC)
\mathcal{B}
, there is a weak Hopf algebra
W
such that
\mathcal{B}
can be realized as weak Hopf lattice gauge theory in the sense that
\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
.

Proof.

1. Combining Lemma
1
and the fact that
\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(W))\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
, we arrive at our conclusion.

2. Given that
\mathcal{B}
is non-chiral, there exists a multifusion category
\mathcal{C}
such that
\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})
. Utilizing Lemma
2
, we can identify a weak Hopf algebra
W
such that
\mathsf{Rep}(W)\simeq\mathcal{C}
. Leveraging the fact
\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(W))\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
, we thus reach our conclusion.
∎

From a given weak Hopf algebra
W
, it is possible to construct a lattice gauge theory with
gauge symmetry

W
, wherein the topological excitations are classified by representations of
D(W)

Jia et al. 2023b
. Consequently,
D(W)
can be viewed as a symmetry, which we will refer to as
charge symmetry
.
As we will elaborate later, the gauge symmetry determines the string types in the multifusion string-net model, whereas the charge symmetry characterizes the topological charges of the model.
Proposition
1
asserts that for non-chiral topological phases, the gauge symmetry and charge symmetry are distinct, they are related by a quantum double operation up to Morita equivalence. Table
2
is a summary of results regarding gauge symmetry and charge symmetry realized by the tube algebras, which will be clarified in Sec.
4
.

2.3
Macroscopic theory of multifusion string-net

Bulk input data

UMFC
\mathcal{D}

Bulk input data

\mathcal{D}
-module
\mathcal{M}

Bulk gauge symmetry

\text{boundary tube algebra}\,\,W_{\rm gauge}\simeq_{\rm w.M.}\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})

Bulk charge symmetry

\text{bulk tube algebra}\,\,W_{\rm charge}\simeq_{\rm s.M.}\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})

Bulk phase

\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})\simeq_{\otimes,\rm br}\mathsf{Rep}(W_{\rm charge})\simeq_{\otimes,\rm br}\mathsf{Rep}(D(W_{\rm gauge}))

Table 2:
The weak Hopf symmetries of the multifusion string-net model. We use “
\simeq_{\rm w.M.}
” to denote weak Morita equivalence, and “
\simeq_{\rm s.M.}
” to denote strong Morita equivalence; “
\simeq_{\otimes}
” to denote monoidal equivalence, and “
\simeq_{\otimes,\rm br}
” to denote braided monoidal equivalence.

Now, let us proceed to develop the macroscopic theory of multifusion string-net for the
2d
bulk,
1d
gapped boundary, and
1d
gapped domain wall.
This subsection serves as a summary of the forthcoming results, offering an overview of the broader picture that will be elucidated later in this work.

Bulk theory.
—
For the
2d
bulk phase, the multifusion string-net model with input UMFC
\mathcal{C}
is equivalent to the lattice gauge theory with a weak Hopf gauge symmetry
W
such that
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(W)
in the sense that they have the same topological excitations
\mathcal{P}\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
.
For lattice gauge theory (denoted as
\mathsf{QD}
, abbreviation of “quantum double”), we have

\text{finite group}~\mathsf{QD}\subset\text{Hopf}~\mathsf{QD}\subset\text{connected weak Hopf}~\mathsf{QD}\subset\text{weak Hopf}~\mathsf{QD}.

(28)

For string-net theory (denoted as
\mathsf{SN}
), we have

\text{Levin-Wen}~\mathsf{SN}\subset\text{multifusion}~\mathsf{SN}.

(29)

When
\mathcal{C}
is a UFC, the gauge symmetry
W
must be a connected weak Hopf algebra, which encompasses all Hopf algebras as examples.
In other words, lattice gauge theories with connected weak Hopf gauge symmetry, including Hopf lattice gauge theories, correspond to Levin-Wen string-net models.
Using results in the previous subsection, we have

\text{multifusion}~\mathsf{SN}\Leftrightarrow\text{weak Hopf}~\mathsf{QD},\quad\text{Levin-Wen}~\mathsf{SN}\Leftrightarrow\text{connected weak Hopf}~\mathsf{QD}.

(30)

This correspondence has been carefully discussed in Refs.
Buerschaper et al. 2013a
;
Meusburger 2017
;
Jia et al. 2023a
for Hopf symmetry.
General lattice gauge theories with (not necessarily connected) weak Hopf gauge symmetry correspond to multifusion string-net models, the lattice realization of this correspondence will be discussed in our future work.

The correspondence between the multifusion string-net model and weak Hopf lattice gauge theory enables us to comprehend the multifusion string-net through the lens of the weak Hopf lattice gauge theory established in our previous work
Jia et al. 2023b
.
A crucial fact of weak Hopf symmetries for a multifusion string-net is that they are not unique.

Definition 5
.

For
2d
topological phases, two weak Hopf gauge symmetries
W
and
W^{\prime}
are called weak Morita equivalent if and only if
\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(W))\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(W^{\prime}))
as UMFCs.
Two weak Hopf charge symmetries
V
and
V^{\prime}
are called strong Morita equivalent if and only if
\mathsf{Rep}(V)\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(V^{\prime})
as braided monoidal categories.

Proposition 2
.

For
2d
topological phases, two weak Hopf gauge symmetries
W
and
W^{\prime}
are weak Morita equivalent if and only if
\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W^{\prime}))
as braided monoidal categories, viz.,
D(W)
and
D(W^{\prime})
are strong Morita equivalent.

Proof.

This arises directly from the fact that
\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(A))\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(A))
as braided monoidal categories for a weak Hopf algebra
A
.
∎

With the groundwork laid out above, we are prepared to summarize our main findings regarding the bulk phase of the multifusion string-net model:

Theorem 1
.

For a multifusion string-net
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
with an input UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, its gauge symmetry is described by a weak Hopf symmetry
W
in the sense that
\mathcal{D}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(W)
as multifusion categories.
The weak Hopf symmetries of a multifusion string-net are not unique, and all these symmetries are Morita equivalent in the sense that
\mathsf{Rep}(W)\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(W^{\prime})\simeq\mathcal{D}
as UMFCs.
The topological excitations of the multifusion string-net model are given by
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
, which is a UMTC. The multifusion string-net model has the same topological excitations as the weak Hopf lattice gauge theory with gauge symmetry given by
W
, for which the topological excitations are given by the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
of the quantum double
D(W)
of
W
. More precisely, this is characterized by
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))
as UMTCs.
This means that the charge symmetry of the multifusion string-net model is given by
D(W)
.
Noticeably, the charge symmetries are not unique; rather, they are Morita equivalent to each other.

Remark 2.2
.

Determining the explicit weak Hopf gauge and charge symmetries for a multifusion string-net is indeed a challenging endeavor. Here we give two approaches:

1.

Tannaka-Krein reconstruction from fiber functor.
— For any UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, there exists a suitable algebra
A
over
\mathbb{C}
such that we can equip
\mathcal{D}
with an exact faithful monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{D}\to{{}_{A}}\mathsf{Mod}_{A}
(called fiber functor over
\mathcal{D}
). The
W=\operatorname{End}(F)
consisting of natural transformations from
F
to itself is an algebra with product given by composition. It can be shown that
W
is a weak Hopf symmetry and
\mathsf{Rep}(W)\simeq\mathcal{D}
as UMFCs
Szlachányi 2001
. This means that
W
is a weak Hopf gauge symmetry for the multifusion string-net
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
.
The charge symmetry of
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
is thus given by
D(W)
.

2.

Tube algebra.
— A more physically intuitive approach is grounded in tube algebra, which will be thoroughly discussed in Sec.
4
. The boundary tube algebra is a weak Hopf symmetry for any gapped boundary of multifusion string-net. If the bulk UMFC is
\mathcal{D}
, we choose the smooth boundary
{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}
and construct the boundary tube algebra
T=\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D})
(see Sec.
5
for details).
The boundary phase is given by the representation category of boundary tube algebra
\mathsf{Rep}(T)
.
Then using the boundary-bulk correspondence, the bulk phase is given by
\mathcal{Z}(\mathsf{Rep}(T))
. This means that we can regard boundary tube algebra
T
as the weak Hopf gauge symmetry for the multifusion string-net
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
.
The weak Hopf charge symmetry is given by the quantum double
D(T)
. Notice that there is another method to construct the weak Hopf charge symmetry directly from the bulk tube algebra
T^{\prime}=\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
, which is strongly Morita equivalent to
D(T)
.
This aspect will be explored in detail in the subsequent sections.

Gapped boundary theory.
—
Utilizing the correspondence between multifusion string-net and lattice gauge theories, we can extend the notion of gauge symmetry and charge symmetry to the
1d
gapped boundary. For a
2d
multifusion string-net with input UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
, the boundary gauge symmetry is characterized by the
W
-comodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
(or equivalently,
W
-module algebra)
Jia et al. 2023b
.
This will be discussed in detail in Sec.
5
.
The category
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod}
of
\mathfrak{A}
-modules is a module category over
\mathcal{D}
.
Via the Kitaev-Kong construction, we obtain a boundary lattice model for multifusion string-net (see Sec.
5
for details).
In general, this gapped boundary phase is a multifusion phase, which is different from the Levin-Wen string-net model.
If the gapped boundary phase is a multifusion phase, it will be referred to as unstable; if it is a fusion phase, it will be referred to as stable.

The gapped boundary theory of the Levin-Wen string-net model can be macroscopically described by anyon condensation theory.
For the gapped boundary of a topological phase with topological excitations characterized by a UMTC
\mathcal{P}
, the gapped boundary is determined by a Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}

Bais et al. 2002
;
Bais et al. 2003
;
Bais and Slingerland 2009
;
Kong 2014
;
Eliëns 2010
;
Burnell 2018
.
The boundary phase is given by the category of
\mathcal{A}
-modules in
\mathcal{P}
, which will be denoted as
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}:={{}_{\mathcal{A}}}\mathsf{Mod}(\mathcal{P})
.
Since
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}
is a
1d
phase, the topological excitations can only fuse but not braid, thus,
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}
is a monoidal category.
It can be proved that the Lagrangian algebra is always simple, thus the boundary phase is always a fusion phase.
For the multifusion string-net, we need to consider the anyon condensation that is described by a disconnected algebra (thus not a Lagrangian algebra)
\mathcal{B}
over a Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}
.
The boundary phase is given by
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}:={{}_{\mathcal{B}}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{P})
, the category of
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules in
\mathcal{P}
. See Sec.
5
for details.

From a symmetry point of view, for the gapped boundary of multifusion string-net
\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
, its boundary gauge symmetry is given by a
W
-comodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
. The category
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod}
of
\mathfrak{A}
-modules is a
\mathcal{C}
-module category.
The boundary charge symmetry is still a weak Hopf algebra
K
for which
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(K)
as monoidal categories.
The
K
and
\mathfrak{A}
is related by a smash product
Jia et al. 2023a
;
Jia et al. 2023b
, and
K

is strongly Morita equivalent to the boundary tube algebra.

Theorem 2
.

There are two equivalent macroscopic descriptions of the gapped boundary theory for multifusion string-net:

1.

Weak Hopf symmetry breaking: For gapped boundary of the multifusion string-net model
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
with
\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
for the gauge weak Hopf symmetry
W
, the boundary gauge symmetry is characterized by a
W
-comodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
. The boundary string labels are given by irreducible
\mathfrak{A}
-modules.
The boundary phase is given by the category of
\mathsf{Rep}(W)
-module functors
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathsf{Rep}(W)}(_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod},_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod})
, which is equivalent to the category
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{W}
of
W
-equivariant
\mathfrak{A}|\mathfrak{A}
-bimodules. The boundary weak Hopf charge symmetry is given by the boundary tube algebra.

2.

Anyon condensation: The gapped boundary is determined by a pair of algebras
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
in the bulk phase
\mathcal{P}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W))\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
, for which
\mathcal{A}
is a Lagrangian algebra and there is an algebra homomorphism
\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
(this makes
\mathcal{B}
an algebra over
\mathcal{A}
). This
\mathcal{B}
is in general disconnected, and the boundary phase is given by the category
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}
of
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules in
\mathcal{P}
.

Remark 2.3
.

A gapped boundary can be regarded as a gapped domain wall that separates a multifusion string-net with the trivial phase
\mathsf{Hilb}
.

Gapped domain wall theory.
—
Consider
2d
topologically ordered phases characterized by UMTCs
\mathcal{P}_{1}
and
\mathcal{P}_{2}
. Via the folding trick, a gapped domain wall separating two phases can be transformed into a gapped boundary of the phase
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
, where
\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
is the same category with
\mathcal{P}_{2}
but equipped with the anti-braiding and “
\boxtimes
” is the Deligne tensor product (physically, it means stacking two topological phases together).
Subsequently, we can employ the gapped boundary theory established above to derive the macroscopic description of gapped domain walls.

From anyon condensation point of view, the gapped domain walls are classified by the Lagrangian algebras
\mathcal{A}
in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
and an algebra
\mathcal{B}
in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
together with an algebra homomorphism
\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
.
The domain wall phase is given by
(\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}})_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}:={{}_{\mathcal{B}}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}})
, the category of
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
.

From a weak Hopf symmetry point of view, for the multifusion string-net model with two UMFCs
\mathcal{C}_{1}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{1})
and
\mathcal{C}_{2}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{2})
, the corresponding bulk phases are Drinfeld centers
\mathcal{P}_{1}=\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C}_{1})
and
\mathcal{P}_{2}=\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C}_{2})
.
The domain wall is characterized by a
\mathcal{C}_{1}|\mathcal{C}_{2}
-bimodule category
\mathcal{M}
.
Via folding trick,
\mathcal{M}
can be regarded as a
\mathcal{C}_{1}\boxtimes\mathcal{C}_{2}^{\rm rev}
-left module category, meaning that it can be regarded as a gapped boundary of the multifusion string-net with input UMFC as
\mathcal{C}_{1}\boxtimes\mathcal{C}_{2}^{\rm rev}
.
Thus we can apply the the boundary theory to obtain the theory of gapped domain wall.
For this case, the corresponding bulk gauge symmetry is
W_{1}\otimes W_{2}^{\rm cop}
, and the domain wall gauge symmetry is a
W_{1}\otimes W_{2}^{\rm cop}
-comodule algebra.
This is equivalent to saying that the domain wall weak Hopf gauge symmetry is characterized by a
W_{1}|W_{2}
-bicomodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
.
The charge symmetry of the gapped domain wall is given by the domain wall tube algebra (see Sec.
6
).

Theorem 3
.

There are two equivalent macroscopic descriptions of the gapped domain wall that separates two multifusion string-net bulks with input UMFCs
\mathcal{D}_{1}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{1})
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{2})
respectively:

1.

Weak Hopf symmetry breaking: For a gapped domain wall with weak Hopf gauge symmetry given by a
W_{1}|W_{2}
-bicomodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
, the category
{{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod}
of left
A
-modules is a
\mathsf{Rep}(W_{1})|\mathsf{Rep}(W_{2})
-bimodule category. The domain wall excitations are given by
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathsf{Rep}(W_{1})|\mathsf{Rep}(W_{2})}({{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod},{{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod})
which is equivalent to
{{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{W_{1}\otimes W_{2}^{\rm cop}}
, the category of
W_{1}\otimes W_{2}^{\rm cop}
-equivariant
\mathfrak{A}|\mathfrak{A}
-bimodules. The charge weak Hopf symmetry is given by the domain wall tube algebra.

2.

Anyon condensation: Two bulk topological phases are given by
\mathcal{P}_{i}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(D(W_{i}))\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i})
with
i=1,2
. The gapped domain wall is characterized by a Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}
in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
together with an algebra
\mathcal{B}
in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
such that there is an algebra homomorphism
\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
. The domain wall excitations are given by
(\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}})_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}:={{}_{\mathcal{B}}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}})
, the category of
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules in
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal{P}_{2}}
.

3
Generalized multifusion string-net model

In this section, we will provide a thorough analysis of the generalized multifusion string-net model.
While we acknowledge that this aspect is well-established among experts, a comprehensive discussion of the multifusion string-net model has been notably absent, except for a succinct mathematical outline provided in Ref.
Chang et al. 2015
. In this section, we endeavor to offer a more elaborate treatment of the subject.

3.1
Input data of multifusion string-net model

Before delving into the intricacies of string-net ground states and lattice Hamiltonians, it is prudent to establish a foundation by elucidating the pertinent input data that will be utilized.
The input data of multifusion string-net model is a UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
for some weak Hopf algebra
W
. It is worth noting that the construction of a string-net model can also be achieved by addressing the self-consistency conditions associated with certain input data.
Throughout this study, we consistently presume the presence of a UMFC as our input data.

Label set and involution.
—
Let
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})=\{X_{i,j}^{k}:k=1,\cdots,n_{i,j},i,j\in I\}
denote the collection of equivalence classes pertaining to simple objects in the category
\mathcal{D}
. A label set
L_{\mathcal{D}}
is the range of an injective map
L:\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})\to\mathbb{N}
.
We will not distinguish
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
and
L_{\mathcal{D}}
in this work and will use them interchangeably whenever there is no risk of ambiguity.
Notice that
L_{\mathcal{D}}
has a grading structure induced by the grading structure of
\mathcal{D}
,
L_{\mathcal{D}}=\sqcup_{i,j}L_{\mathcal{D}_{i,j}}
.
For UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
, we denote the label set of all objects
\mathbf{1}_{i}
,
i\in I
, as
L_{\mathcal{D}}^{0}
.
The rigidity structure induces an involution on
L_{\mathcal{D}}
,
*:L_{\mathcal{D}}\to L_{\mathcal{D}}
.
For
X\in L_{\mathcal{D}}^{0}
,
X^{*}=X
; for
X\in L_{\mathcal{D}_{i,j}}
,
X^{*}\in L_{\mathcal{D}_{j,i}}
.

Fusion rule and quantum dimension.
—
The fusion rule of
\mathcal{D}
is a map
N:L_{\mathcal{D}}\times L_{\mathcal{D}}\times L_{\mathcal{D}}\to\mathbb{N}
, which is induced by the fusion structure of
\mathcal{D}
,
X\otimes Y=\oplus_{Z\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}N_{X,Y}^{Z}Z
.
The fusion rule is associative in the sense that
\sum_{Z\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}N_{X,Y}^{Z}N_{Z,W}^{V}=\sum_{Z\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}N_{X,Z}^{V}N_{Y,W}^{Z}
.
The fusion rule is not commutative in general:
N_{X,Y}^{Z}\neq N_{Y,X}^{Z}
.
For an object
X
, if we regard
N_{X,Y}^{Z}
as a matrix with entries
[N_{X}]_{Y}^{Z}=N_{X,Y}^{Z}
, then from the Frobenius-Perron theorem
Etingof et al. 2005
we know that the largest eigenvalue is always positive; this number is defined as the quantum dimension of
X
and denoted as
d_{X}
. The total quantum dimension of
\mathcal{D}
is defined as
d_{\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{X\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}d_{X}^{2}
.
\mathcal{D}
is called multiplicity-free if the fusion coefficient
N_{X,Y}^{Z}\in\{0,1\}
for all simple objects
X,Y,Z
.

Local normalization and local evaluation.
—
In a diagrammatic representation, each edge is represented as a line directing upwards, which is similar to anyon worldline. For fusion/splitting, there are associated vector spaces
V_{c}^{ab}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(c,a\otimes b)
and
V_{ab}^{c}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(a\otimes b,c)
spanned by the fusion/splitting vertex vectors. To normalize these local vertex vectors, we can introduce a factor
Y_{c}^{ab}
in the following manner:

(36)

Typically, the choice for
Y^{ab}_{c}
is made as
(d_{a}d_{b}/d_{c})^{1/2}
. It is noteworthy that this corresponds to a specific gauge selection.

F-symbols and evaluation.
—
The associativity isomorphism
a:(i\otimes j)\otimes k\to i\otimes(j\otimes k)
induces a linear map
F_{l}^{ijk}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(l,(i\otimes j)\otimes k)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(l,i\otimes(j\otimes k))
. Similarly,
a^{\dagger}
induces
(F_{l}^{ijk})^{\dagger}
. Since
\mathcal{D}
is unitary, we have
(F_{l}^{ijk})^{\dagger}=(F_{l}^{ijk})^{-1}
. Diagrammatically, these maps are called F-moves:

(40)

The associator in UMFC adheres to the pentagon relation, as depicted in Fig.
1
. In explicit terms, this relationship is expressed as

\displaystyle\sum_{\mu}[F_{a}^{mkl}]_{n\alpha\beta}^{b\mu\nu}[F_{a}^{ijb}]_{m\mu\gamma}^{c\sigma\zeta}=\sum_{d,\lambda,\tau,\nu}[F_{n}^{ijk}]^{d\lambda\tau}_{m\beta\gamma}[F_{a}^{idl}]^{c\sigma\eta}_{n\alpha\lambda}[F_{c}^{jkl}]_{d\tau\eta}^{b\zeta\nu}.

(41)

Since
\mathcal{D}
is unitary, the F-matrix can also be chosen as a unitary matrix

(F_{l}^{ijk})^{\dagger}=(F_{l}^{ijk})^{-1}.

(42)

The F-symbols exhibit a mirror conjugate symmetry, a property pivotal for the construction of the Levin-Wen model with a boundary. By drawing parallels to the methods outlined in Ref.
Hong 2009
, we can demonstrate that

\sum_{n,\mu,\nu}[F_{l}^{ijk}]_{m\alpha\beta}^{n\mu\nu}[F^{l}_{ijk}]_{m^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime}\beta^{\prime}}^{n\mu\nu}=\delta_{m,m^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}}\delta_{\beta,\beta^{\prime}}.

(43)

Figure 1:
Pentagon relation for the F-symbols.

Proposition 3
.

The loop move, parallel move, and F-move, collectively known as topological local moves, are equivalent to the Pachner moves.

Proof.

This can be demonstrated in a manner similar to the fusion category case. See Refs.
Hu et al. 2012
;
Hu et al. 2018
.

Definition 6

(Input data)
.

The input data for the generalized multifusion string-net are:

1.

String type:
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
;

2.

Fusion rule:
N_{a,b}^{c}

7
7

7

Recall that the quantum dimensions
d_{a}
’s are determined by the fusion rule.

Y_{c}^{ab}

Remark 3.1

(Tetrahedral symmetry)
.

The original Levin-Wen string-net model requires that F-symbols satisfy the tetrahedral symmetry
Levin and Wen 2005
;
Chang et al. 2015
.
However, it is known that not all UMFCs allow F-symbols that have tetrahedral symmetry
Turaev 2016
;
Hong 2009
;
Fuchs and Grøsfjeld 2023
. For the unimodal ribbon category, Turaev proved that it is always possible to have tetrahedral symmetric F-symbols
Turaev 2016
. Recently, a more comprehensive understanding of the tetrahedral symmetry is provided in Ref.
Fuchs and Grøsfjeld 2023
.

3.2
Generalized multifusion string-net ground states

Imagine a connected oriented trivalent lattice
\Sigma
, called a string-net
8
8

8

It is worth noting that bivalent vertices are permissible, provided one of the edges is designated as vacant edge
\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{D}
. Given that vacant edges can be arbitrarily added or removed, this does not alter the model’s fundamentals.
, situated on a spatial
2d
-manifold.
We will assume that the string-net forms a cellulation of the given surface and denote the sets of vertices, edges and faces as
C^{k}(\Sigma)
,
k=0,1,2
respectively.
A
generalized string-net
is characterized by edges that are oriented in either an upward or downward direction
9
9

9

Using the Whitney embedding theorem, the string-net can be embedded into
\mathbb{R}^{N}
, allowing for the definition of the up or down direction in relation to a specified axis.
It is also noteworthy that, we only consider the spatial manifold
\Sigma
, for which a trivalent lattice can always be identified on it.

. See Fig.
2
for an illustration.
In this lattice, the physical degrees of freedom are located on its edges and vertices.
We label edges with simple objects in
\mathcal{D}
and vertices with morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
.
The Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
is spanned by all configurations of the labels on edges and vertices.

In a graphical representation, each bulk edge is labeled by elements in
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
, and if we reverse the direction of one edge labeled by
k
, then the label should be replaced by
k^{*}
.
The vacant edge, which is usually drawn as dotted line or is invisible, is labeled by
\mathds{1}_{i}
. To summarize:

(46)

It is important to observe that in multifusion string-net models, vacant edges are represented by a set of edge labels denoted as
\mathbf{1}_{i}
, where
i\in I
. Unlike the case of original fusion string-nets, the addition or removal of vacant edges is constrained. Specifically, the condition
\mathbf{1}_{i}\otimes X\neq 0
holds only when
X\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D}_{i,j})
. Thus, the inclusion or exclusion of vacant edges is subject to the grading structure imposed by the UMFC
\mathcal{D}
.

The trivalent vertices are labeled by morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
.

(47)

Notice that here for
a\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
and
b\in\mathcal{D}_{k,l}
, the morphism is nonzero only if
j=k
and
c\in\mathcal{D}_{i,l}
.
When
c=\mathbf{1}_{i}
,
a\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
and
b=a^{*}\in\mathcal{D}_{j,i}
, the vertex becomes bivalent.

Definition 7

(Inner product of vertex morphisms)
.

For the vertex morphisms
\mu,\nu\in V_{c}^{ab}
we define their Markov inner product via stacking two vertex diagrams corresponding to
\mu
and
\nu^{\dagger}
together

(48)

The Markov trace provided in Eq. (
45
) can be applied to both sides of the preceding expression, resulting in an equivalent definition. This justifies the term “Markov inner product”.
In juxtaposition with the standard inner product presented in Eqs. (
33
) and (
34
), the sole discrepancy lies in a fixed factor incorporating the quantum dimensions associated with the edge labels.
We will interchangeably use these terms, following the convention that the vertex labels
\alpha\in V_{c}^{ab}
, with
\beta\in V_{ab}^{c}
(treated as
\beta=\gamma^{\dagger}
, where
\gamma\in V_{c}^{ab}
), are chosen to ensure mutual duality.

We can introduce a tensor product structure for generalized multifusion string-net as follows. The total Hilbert space is defined as
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tot}}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]=\otimes_{v\in{C}^{0}(\Sigma)}\mathcal{H}_{v}
, where
{C}^{k}(\Sigma)
denotes the set of
k
-cells in a lattice, and
\mathcal{H}_{v}=\oplus_{a,b,c\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}V_{c}^{ab}
or
\oplus_{a,b,c\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}V^{c}_{ab}
, depending on the shape of
v
.
We can introduce edge projectors
E_{e}
on the space
\mathcal{H}_{v_{1}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{v_{2}}
, where
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
represent adjacent vertices connected by
e
, in the following manner:

E_{e}(|a,b\rightarrow c;\alpha\rangle\otimes|i\rightarrow j,k;\beta\rangle)=\delta_{c,i}|a,b\rightarrow c;\alpha\rangle\otimes|c\rightarrow j,k;\beta\rangle.

(49)

We call a string-net labeling
|S\rangle
stable if the labels on incident edges match with each other,
viz.
,
|S\rangle\in(\otimes_{e\in C^{1}(\Sigma)}E_{e})\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tot}}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
. The space generated by all stable labeling is the physical space
\mathcal{H}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]\hookrightarrow\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{tot}}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
.

A fully labeled string-net is viewed as a specific composition of morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
, with its domain being the tensor product of all incoming edge labels, and its codomain being the tensor product of all outgoing edge labels. In contrast, a partially labeled string-net symbolizes the projection of the ground state subspace onto the subspace of
\mathcal{H}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
where the states maintain fixed labels on the labeled vertices and edges.

Since a fully labeled string-net can be regarded as a composition of morphisms in the multifusion category
\mathcal{D}
, the graphical calculus of multifusion category
\mathcal{D}
can be applied in the Hilbert space.
It turns out that the topological features of the string-net gapped boundary wavefunction can be captured by some local evaluations of the string-net with boundary, which can be regarded as a state renormalization procedure.
When applying state renormalization, the lattice on which the string-net is defined will change.
Nevertheless, we still can hope that the ground state space remains unchanged, since string-net state is a fixed-point state under renormalization.
This leads us to compare the ground state spaces corresponding to different graphs.
Consider two graphs
\Sigma_{1}
and
\Sigma_{2}
which only differ in some local area and the corresponding total Hilbert spaces
\mathcal{H}_{1}
and
\mathcal{H}_{2}
satisfy
\dim\mathcal{H}_{1}\geq\dim\mathcal{H}_{2}
; if two lattices can be renormalized into the same fixed-point class, the respective invariant ground state subspaces
\mathcal{K}_{1}
and
\mathcal{K}_{2}
are isomorphic.
An evaluation
\mathrm{ev}:\mathcal{H}_{1}\to\mathcal{H}_{2}
is a linear map which is identity map on the overlapping part of two graphs and is unitary when restricted on
\mathcal{K}_{1}
. The evaluation reduces some freedom of the system thus represents the renormalization procedure of the states.

The equations (
34
), (
36
), and the F-moves specified in Eqs. (
37
)-(
40
) are referred to as
topological local moves
.
By employing these topological local moves, we can construct string-net ground states characterized by their topological nature, representing fixed-point states.

The ground state can be expressed as
|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{X}\Psi(X)|X\rangle
, where the
|X\rangle
’s represent string-net configurations and the
\Psi(X)
’s are the corresponding complex coefficients.
Notice that
|X\rangle
contains all the edge labels
a_{e}\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
with
e\in C^{1}({\Sigma})
and vertex labels
\alpha_{v}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}
with
v\in C^{0}(\Sigma)
; a more explicit notation should be
|X(a_{e},\alpha_{v});e\in C^{1}({\Sigma}),v\in C^{0}(\Sigma)\rangle
. A string-net configuration represents a composition of vertex morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
,
viz.
,
X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})=\alpha_{n}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\cdots\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\alpha_{1}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}
.
The dual vector
\langle X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})|
can be regarded as the dual morphism of
X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})
,
viz.
,
X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})^{\dagger}=\alpha_{1}^{\dagger}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\cdots\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\alpha_{n}^{\dagger}
.
The Definition
7
of vertex morphisms can thus be generalized to the string-net configurations:

Definition 8

(Inner product of generalized multifusion string-net configurations)
.

For two string-net configurations
X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})
and
Y(b_{e},\beta_{v})
in
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(i_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes i_{s},j_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes j_{s})
, we define their inner product via stacking the morphisms
X(a_{e},\alpha_{v})
and
Y(b_{e},\beta_{v})^{\dagger}=Y(b_{e},\beta_{v}^{\dagger})
.

(50)

We can take Markov trace for both sides of the above expression to obtain an equivalent definition.

Thus to determine the state, we only need to determine
\Psi(X)
.
This can be done by fixing the convention that
\Psi(\text{vac})=1
and using the local evaluations to transform all the configurations into the vacant string-net.
Here by vacant string-net we mean a morphism from
\mathbf{1}
to
\mathbf{1}
in the UMFC
\mathcal{D}
. Indeed, the vacant configuration in the UMFC context is nuanced due to the complexity introduced by the fact that
\mathbf{1}
is no longer a simple object.
Taking a disk as an example (see Fig.
5
), a fully labeled string-net can be regarded as a morphism from
\mathbf{1}_{j}
to
\mathbf{1}_{j}
. Every string-net configuration can be transformed into the vacant configuration via the local moves.

Figure 2:
Depiction of the generalized multifusion string-net.

3.3
Generalized multifusion string-net lattice Hamiltonian

Having introduced the construction of a generalized multifusion string-net ground state, this subsection will focus on the development of the corresponding lattice Hamiltonian.

For a given vertex in the generalized multifusion string-net, we define
\delta_{a,b\to c}=1
if
V_{ab}^{c}\neq 0
; otherwise, we set
\delta_{a,b\to c}=0
. Similarly
\delta_{c\to a,b}
is defined. Using these, we introduce a vertex projector
Q_{v}

(51)

The condition
Q_{v}=1
corresponds to satisfying Gauss’s law at the vertex
v
in an analogy with lattice gauge theory.

The face operator
B_{f}
is more complicated. It is a linear combination of some basic face operators
B^{k}_{f}
:

B_{f}=\sum_{k\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}w_{k}B^{k}_{f},

(52)

where
w_{k}=Y^{k^{*}k}_{\mathbf{1}}/\sum_{l\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}d_{l}^{2}
. By selecting the gauge as
Y^{ab}_{c}=(d_{a}d_{b}/d_{c})^{1/2}
, we observe that this aligns with the gauge choice conventionally made in the original string-net model.
The face operator
B_{f}^{k}
acts on the face of the string-net by inserting a
k
-loop into the face
f
, which graphically looks like

(53)

It is noteworthy that, commonly, a hexagon is considered as an illustrative example, while the face operator is designed to act on a face with an arbitrary number of edges.
The condition
B_{f}=1
can be conceptualized as ensuring that no flux penetrates the face
f
.

Proposition 4
.

The local stabilizers
Q_{v}
and
B_{f}
functions are projectors and mutually commute. Consequently, the Hamiltonian of the generalized multifusion string-net
10
10

10

The Hamiltonian is formulated on the space
\mathcal{H}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
, encompassing string-nets with stable labelings. To emphasize the tensor product structure, one can define the Hamiltonian in the total space
\mathcal{H}_{\rm tot}[\Sigma,\mathcal{D}]
, wherein the Hamiltonian incorporates edge projectors as well:
H=-J_{e}\sum_{e}E_{e}-J_{v}\sum_{v}Q_{v}-J_{f}\sum_{f}B_{f}
.
(
J_{v},J_{f}>0
)

H=-J_{v}\sum_{v}Q_{v}-J_{f}\sum_{f}B_{f}

(54)

being a local commutative projector (LCP) Hamiltonian, exhibits a gap in the thermodynamic limit.

Proof.

By definition, we see that the
Q_{v}
’s are projectors and
[Q_{v},Q_{v^{\prime}}]=0
for all distinct vertices
v
and
v^{\prime}
.

Using the same method as in Refs.
Hong 2009
;
Hahn and Wolf 2020
, we can show that

(B_{f}^{k})^{\dagger}=B^{k^{*}}_{f}.

(55)

Notice that the main trick here is to use the inner product that we introduced in Definitions
7
and
