(56)

where the first identity is from Eq. (
36
), and the third from Eq. (
34
). Using these facts one can show that the
B_{f}
’s are projectors.
∎

Proposition 5
.

The generalized multifusion string-net ground state
|\Psi\rangle
constructed in the previous subsection is invariant under the action of
Q_{v}
and
B_{f}
for all vertices
v
and faces
f
.

Proof.

The condition
Q_{v}|\Psi\rangle=|\Psi\rangle
is clear from the definition.
To show that
|\Psi\rangle
is stabilized by all
B_{f}
’s, we claim that

B_{f}^{a}=Y^{aa^{*}}_{\mathbf{1}_{i}}

(57)

for
a\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
. Then from the definition of
B_{f}
we derive
B_{f}|\Psi\rangle=|\Psi\rangle
.
To show the claim, consider the string-net configuration
\langle S|
, we see that

\langle S|B_{f}^{a}|\Psi\rangle=\langle B_{f}^{a^{*}}S|\Psi\rangle=Y^{aa^{*}}_{\mathbf{1}_{i}}\langle S|\Psi\rangle,

(58)

where we have used Eqs. (
34
) and (
55
). This proves the claim.
∎

3.4
Topological ground state degeneracy

The simplest topological observable of the topological ordered phase is the ground state degeneracy.
For the original Levin-Wen string-net model, we know that it depends on the topology of the spatial manifold and the input UFC.
The ground state degeneracies for the Levin-Wen string-net model have been computed in prior works
Hu et al. 2012
;
Vidal 2022
;
Ritz-Zwilling et al. 2024
.

A parallel observation holds for the multifusion string-net model. The ground state degeneracy in the generalized multifusion string-net model remains a topological invariant, resilient to topological local moves.
Using the local stabilizers, the ground state degeneracy can be expressed as

\operatorname{GSD}=\operatorname{Tr}\left(\prod_{v}Q_{v}\right)\left(\prod_{f}B_{f}\right).

(59)

For a given spatial manifold, the calculation of the
\operatorname{GSD}
involves evaluating it through the consideration of the simplest cellulation of the manifold and using the fact that
\operatorname{GSD}
is a topological invariant.

Moore-Seiberg formula
Moore and Seiberg 1989
;
Ritz-Zwilling et al. 2024
of
\operatorname{GSD}
also holds for the generalized multifusion string-net model (with an input indecomposable UMFC
\mathcal{D}
), since the topological excitations still form a UMTC (see Theorem
1
).
Consider an orientable
g
-genus surface
\Sigma_{g,k}
with
k
punctures, we can assign anyons (simple objects in
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
) to the punctures of the surface, denoted as
X_{1},\cdots,X_{k}
. The following is an example with 6 anyons on a
3
-genus surface:

This surface can be decomposed into pant surfaces that are subsequently glued together. It is essential to note that this decomposition is not unique in general, but the associativity of fusion of anyons guarantees that the final result for GSD is the same:

\operatorname{GSD}[\Sigma_{g,k},X_{1},\cdots,X_{k}]=\sum_{Y\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}))}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{k}S_{X_{j},Y}\right)S_{\mathbf{1},Y}^{2-2g-k},

(60)

where
S
is the S-matrix,
\mathbf{1}
is the vacuum charge (tensor unit of
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
),
g
is the number of genus, and
k
is the number of punctures.
When there are no punctures, we obtain the expression of the GSD for multifusion string-net model:

\operatorname{GSD}[\Sigma_{g}]=\operatorname{GSD}[\Sigma_{g,k},X_{1}=\cdots=X_{k}=\mathbf{1}]=\sum_{Y\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}))}S_{\mathbf{1},Y}^{2-2g}.

(61)

It is crucial to observe that the expression (
60
) is not applicable in scenarios involving excitations. This limitation arises from the existence of additional fusion channels, as detailed in
Ritz-Zwilling et al. 2024
.

4
Weak Hopf tube algebra and topological excitations

In this section, we present an approach to investigate and classify the topological excitations in a multifusion string-net model.
We will use the string diagram calculus to construct a tube algebra and show that the tube algebra is a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra.
This can be regarded as a generalization of Ocneanu’s tube algebra
Ocneanu 1994
;
Ocneanu 2001
.
It is worth noting that our approach differs from the Q-algebra approach for Levin-Wen string-net proposed in Ref.
Lan and Wen 2014
, where the Q-algebra lacks a coalgebra structure.
Our construction of the bulk tube algebra exhibits another interesting property: the Kitaev-Kong boundary tube algebra (denoted as
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{M})
in our notation, see Sec.
5
for a detailed discussion) constructed in Ref.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
can be naturally embedded into it. Furthermore, intriguingly, we can consider its dual weak Hopf algebra as a mirror reflection of the diagram corresponding to
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{M})
. This reflection reveals that their crossed multiplication aligns well with the bulk tube algebra.
Notice that hereinafter, whenever necessary to stress the base UMFC category, we will denote a left (resp. right)
\mathcal{D}
-module category by
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}
(resp.
\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}}
), and a
\mathcal{C}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule category by
{{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}}
.

The ground state space of multifusion string-net model consists of translational invariant constant energy density states which satisfy stabilizer conditions:
Q_{v}|\Psi\rangle=|\Psi\rangle
and
B_{f}|\Psi\rangle=|\Psi\rangle
for all
v\in C^{0}(\Sigma)
and
f\in C^{2}(\Sigma)
.
For a local connected region of string-net, if the stabilizers in this region do not stabilize the state, then we say that there are excitations inside the region.
We call a state
|\Phi\rangle
whereby
Q_{v}|\Psi\rangle=0
an electric charge excitation; we call a state
|\Phi\rangle
whereby
B_{f}|\Psi\rangle=0
a magnetic flux excitation; if
Q_{v}|\Psi\rangle=0=B_{f}|\Psi\rangle
, we call them dyonic charge excitations.
Due to their topological nature, we can explore how to shrink or enlarge the excited region. This perspective leads us to the concept of the tube algebra, which establishes connections between the excited region and the unexcited region.
We will show that the excitations are modules of the tube algebra.
The coalgebra action can also be understood naturally in this framework.

4.1
Bulk tube algebra as weak Hopf algebra

Figure 3:
Depiction of the tube algebra.

For a generalized string-net
\Sigma
, consider a disk region
\Gamma\subset\Sigma
which consists of a connected set of vertices. This means that we always cut the disk region for a string-net along the edges,
resulting in a boundary comprising a collection of faces. It is crucial to recall that, in constructing our generalized multifusion string-net, a tensor product structure is assigned to each edge, with the edge projector ensuring the alignment of the two labels on the same edge.
The boundary
\partial\Gamma
of
\Gamma
are edges that connect the vertices inside
\Gamma
and that outside
\Gamma
.
See Fig.
3
for an illustration.
For
e\in\partial\Gamma
, we denote
\partial_{i}e
and
\partial_{o}e
the vertices of
e
inside and outside
\Gamma
, respectively. A tube region
\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
surrounding
\Gamma
consists of vertices
\partial_{o}e
for all
e\in\partial\Gamma
, along with vertices that form the shortest connected path in
\Sigma
containing all
\partial_{o}e
for
e\in\partial\Gamma
.
The boundary edges of
\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
can be divided into two groups:

\partial_{i}\!\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
consisting of all edges that connect
\Gamma
, and

\partial_{o}\!\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
consisting of all edges that outside the
\Gamma\cup\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
.

Consider the disk region
\Gamma\subset\Sigma
, we have Hamiltonian for this disk

H[\Gamma]=-\sum_{v\in\Gamma}Q_{v}-\sum_{f\in\Gamma}B_{f}.

(62)

Notice that the boundary faces of
\Gamma
are not contained in the above Hamiltonian, thus
H[\Gamma]
is an open-boundary Hamiltonian.
This implies that we have a natural decomposition of the ground state space for
H[\Gamma]
:
\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}[\Gamma]=\bigoplus_{C_{\rm bd}}\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}[\Gamma]_{C_{\rm bd}}
with “
C_{\rm bd}
” represents the open-boundary conditions.
When we consider the topological properties of the excitations in
\Gamma
, a crucial observation is that the disk region is unchanged under gluing a tube:

This means that we can topologically enlarge the disk
\Gamma
to
\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma\cup\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
.
The excitations for
H[\Gamma^{\prime}]
and
H[\Gamma]
are topologically equivalent.
From the algebraic point of view, this means that there is an action of tube over the disk.
Consider a general tube
\operatorname{Tube}
, it has two boundaries, both of the boundaries consist of collections of boundary faces. We can also construct a Hamiltonian for the tube

H[\operatorname{Tube}]=-\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Tube}}Q_{v}-\sum_{f\in\operatorname{Tube}}B_{f},

(63)

where by
v\in\operatorname{Tube}
and
f\in\operatorname{Tube}
we mean the vertices and faces that fully contained in
\operatorname{Tube}
.
The tube ground state space will also have decomposition depending on the choices of open-boundary conditions for two boundaries
\partial_{0}\!\operatorname{Tube}
and
\partial_{1}\!\operatorname{Tube}
:

\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}[\operatorname{Tube}]=\bigoplus_{\partial_{0}\!\operatorname{Tube},\,\partial_{1}\!\operatorname{Tube}}\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}[\operatorname{Tube}]_{\partial_{0}\!\operatorname{Tube},\,\partial_{1}\!\operatorname{Tube}}.

(64)

Consider a domain wall that separates two multifusion string-net phases with input UMFCs
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
, respectively. Based on the Kitaev-Kong construction
Kitaev and Kong 2012
, we know that the domain wall is characterized by a
\mathcal{C}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule category
\mathcal{M}
.
Suppose that there is a disk region
\Gamma
across the domain wall where the stabilizer conditions do not hold for vertices and faces inside the region. Due to the topological nature of the string-net model, we can deform the tube region and
\Gamma
using the topological local moves such that the tube region only consists of domain wall vertices and the boundary of excited region only consists of two domain wall edges (see Fig.
3
).
Each tube vertex corresponds to a morphism space in the bimodule category. By taking the tensor product of these vertex spaces while applying the edge stability condition, we naturally obtain a vector space. This vector space will be denoted as
\mathbf{Tube}(_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}})
.
We will demonstrate that this vector space forms an algebra, and the wall excitations are modules over this algebra.
Let us first consider a special case of trivial domain wall (viewing
\mathcal{D}
as a
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule).
The topological excitations of the multifusion string-net model can be regarded as a point defect over trivial domain walls.

(65)

Note that the arrows have been omitted to avoid clutter in the equation; all edges are assumed to be directed upwards. Also, observe that these basis elements must adhere to the graded fusion rule of
\mathcal{D}
, namely, the following fusions must be nonzero:
a\otimes e
,
d\otimes b
,
a\otimes f
,
g\otimes b
.

It is clear that the dimension of
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
is equal to

\dim\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})=\sum_{a,\cdots,h\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})}N_{c}^{db}N_{d}^{ae}N_{af}^{g}N_{gb}^{h}.

(66)

where the dotted line represents the tensor unit
\mathbf{1}
. It is worth noting that from Eq. (
65
), these dotted lines indeed represent
\mathbf{1}_{i}
, where
i\in I
depending on the choices of
a,b\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
. For example, if
a,b\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
, the left dotted line represents
\mathbf{1}_{i}
and the right dotted line represents
\mathbf{1}_{j}
.

From the definition, it is evident that multiplication is associative, as the diagrams for both
(\bullet\cdot\bullet)\cdot\bullet
and
\bullet\cdot(\bullet\cdot\bullet)
are the same. The unit property follows directly from the definition.

65
) as
[a;b]_{c,d,e;\mu,\nu}^{f,g,h;\zeta,\gamma}

[a,a^{\prime};b^{\prime},b]_{c,d,c^{\prime},d^{\prime},e^{\prime};\mu,\nu,\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}^{f^{\prime},g^{\prime},h^{\prime},g,h;\zeta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime},\zeta,\gamma}
.

.

(69)

It can be easily verified that this is indeed a module action by using the topological local moves.
We observe that the physical properties of a given region
\Gamma
are encoded in the boundary conditions of the region. State renormalization allows us to treat the excited region as a left module over the tube algebra. The topological charges are classified by the irreducible representations of the tube algebra. We can also examine the relationship between the excited region before and after the topological local moves; as we will show later, their corresponding tube algebras are Morita equivalent.

Before we discuss the representation theory of the tube algebra, let us first construct the coalgebra structure for the tube algebra. Suppose there are two excited regions on the domain wall; we can consider the action of the tube algebra over these two regions.
Using parallel evaluation, we obtain the following:

(72)

i
and the coefficient factors, this means that we insert an

and

and

, then for

and

.

Remark 4.1
.

A direct observation is that when taking
\varepsilon
for the product in equality (
68
), it does not matter to complete the second or third diagram (up to a factor
1/d_{h}
). More precisely, to compute
\varepsilon(XY)
for
X=[a;b]_{c,d,e;\mu,\nu}^{f,g,h;\zeta,\gamma}
and
Y=[a^{\prime};b^{\prime}]_{c^{\prime},d^{\prime},e^{\prime};\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}^{f^{\prime},g^{\prime},h^{\prime};\zeta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime}}
, we can first stack the diagrams, and then complete the resulting diagram in the following sense:

Proposition 8

For any given UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, the tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
constitutes a weak bialgebra with the previously given structure morphisms
\mu,1,\Delta,\varepsilon
.

\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,k,\rho,\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{d_{a^{\prime}}d_{i}}}\sqrt{\frac{d_{k}}{d_{j}d_{b^{\prime}}}}\delta_{f,h^{\prime}}\delta_{e,k}\delta_{i,h^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{e^{\prime},c^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{i,f^{\prime}}\delta_{c,h}\delta_{e^{\prime\prime},f^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{c^{\prime},k}\frac{1}{d_{h}}\frac{1}{d_{k}}

\displaystyle\quad\quad\delta_{\nu^{\prime\prime},\zeta^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{\mu^{\prime\prime},\gamma^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{\nu^{\prime},\sigma}\delta_{\mu^{\prime},\rho}\delta_{d^{\prime\prime},g^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{e^{\prime},i}\delta_{d^{\prime},j}\sqrt{d_{a^{\prime}}d_{a^{\prime\prime}}d_{e^{\prime\prime}}d_{b^{\prime}}d_{b^{\prime\prime}}d_{k}}

\displaystyle=\delta_{f,h^{\prime}}\delta_{e,c^{\prime}}\delta_{f^{\prime},h^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{e^{\prime},c^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{c,h}\delta_{e^{\prime\prime},f^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{\nu,\zeta}\delta_{\mu,\gamma}\delta_{\nu^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime}}\delta_{\mu^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime}}\delta_{\nu^{\prime\prime},\zeta^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{\mu^{\prime\prime},\gamma^{\prime\prime}}

\displaystyle\quad\quad\delta_{d^{\prime\prime},g^{\prime\prime}}\delta_{e^{\prime},f^{\prime}}\delta_{d^{\prime},g^{\prime}}\delta_{e,f}\delta_{d,g}\sqrt{\frac{d_{a}d_{a^{\prime}}d_{a^{\prime\prime}}d_{e^{\prime\prime}}d_{b}d_{b^{\prime}}d_{b^{\prime\prime}}}{d_{h}}},

as desired. Similarly, one has
\varepsilon(XYZ)=\sum_{(Y)}\varepsilon(XY^{(2)})\varepsilon(Y^{(1)}Z)
. ∎

Before we proceed to construct the weak Hopf algebra structure of the tube algebra, it is worth discussing the left and right counital maps. Recall that by definition, the left and the right counital maps are

\varepsilon_{L}(X)=\sum_{(1)}\varepsilon(1^{(1)}\cdot X)1^{(2)}\quad\text{and}\quad\varepsilon_{R}(X)=\sum_{(1)}1^{(1)}\varepsilon(X\cdot 1^{(2)}),

respectively. Using the coproduct of the unit given by Eq. (

Remark 4.2
.

For
X=[a;b]_{c,d,e;\mu,\nu}^{f,g,h;\zeta,\gamma}
, when computing
S^{2}(X)
, one first needs to rewrite the right-hand side of Eq. (
77

(81)

Therefore, one has
S^{2}(X)=(d_{f}d_{c}/d_{h}d_{e})X
by inspecting the diagrams. This means that
S^{2}\neq\mathrm{id}
in general, which is different from the Hopf algebra case.
For a general weak Hopf algebra
W
, there exists a grouplike element
\xi\in W
such that
S^{2}(h)=\xi h\xi^{-1}
holds for all
h\in W
. For the tube algebra, we can write down a grouplike element which realizes this condition. In fact, this grouplike element
\xi
of
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})

A
*
-weak Hopf algebra is a weak Hopf algebra
W
equipped with a
C^{*}
structure
*:W\to W
such that
\Delta
is a
*
-homomorphism. In other words,

(x^{*})^{*}=x,\,(x+y)^{*}=x^{*}+y^{*},\,(xy)^{*}=y^{*}x^{*},\,(\alpha x)^{*}=\bar{\alpha}x^{*},

(83)

and

\Delta(x)^{*}=\Delta(x^{*}),

(84)

hold for all
x,y\in W
and
\alpha\in\mathbb{C}
. Additionally, it is shown that
S(x^{*})=S^{-1}(x)^{*}
. Note that the antipode
S
is invertible.
The term
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra is used if there exists a fully faithful
*
-representation
\rho:W\to\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{H})
for some operator space over a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
. Notice that a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra is semisimple.
Let us now demonstrate that we can establish a
C^{*}
structure over the tube algebra.

Proposition 10
.

For any given UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, the tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
is a
C^{*}

weak Hopf algebra. The
*
-operation is given by

(85)

The morphisms on the right-hand side should be interpreted as the dual morphisms corresponding to the respective vertices.

Proof.

Fix
X=[a;b]_{c,d,e;\mu,\nu}^{f,g,h;\zeta,\gamma}
and
Y=[a^{\prime};b^{\prime}]_{c^{\prime},d^{\prime},e^{\prime};\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}}^{f^{\prime},g^{\prime},h^{\prime};\zeta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime}}
in
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
. Note that the
*
-operation in Eq. (
85
) is extended antilinearly, thus
(\alpha X)^{*}=\bar{\alpha}X^{*}
for
\alpha\in\mathbb{C}
. It is clear that
(X^{*})^{*}=X
,
(X+Y)^{*}=X^{*}+Y^{*}
. It remains to show that
(XY)^{*}=Y^{*}X^{*}
and
\Delta(X)^{*}=\Delta(X^{*})
. The first identity holds because of the following

(86)

Actually we have used this fact while we showed that
*
-operation is involutive. It follows that
S(S(X^{*})^{*})=X
, namely
S(X^{*})=S^{-1}(X)^{*}
, holds for any
X\in\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
, which is consistent with the property for general weak Hopf algebras.

Remark 4.4
.

It is worth noting that the coefficients chosen in the above definitions are not unique. We can apply local basis transformations and obtain new structure coefficients from the given ones.

4.2
Tube algebra as a crossed product

Since we are working on the trivial domain wall
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
, which forms a bimodule category over itself, if we disregard the right module structure, we obtain the following subalgebra:

(87)

From the discussion in the previous subsection, it is clear that
\mathbf{L}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})
is a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra.
It is isomorphic to the boundary tube algebra that will be discussed in Sec.
5
. The boundary tube algebra is originally constructed in Ref.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
. Note that the structure coefficient we choose here is slightly different from that of Ref.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
; also, refer to Ref.
Bridgeman et al. 2023
for a discussion, where the algebra is named annular algebra.
As will be discussed later in Sec.
5
, this boundary tube algebra gives the boundary excitations (regard
\mathcal{D}
as a left
\mathcal{D}
-module category):
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}}))
; see Sec.
5
for the definition of
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})
. Eq. (
87
) provides a natural embedding of boundary tube algebra to the bulk tube algebra:
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})\cong\mathbf{L}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
.

C^{*}
weak Hopf subalgebra:

We also have the embedding:
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}({\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})\cong\mathbf{R}({\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
; see Sec.

for the definition of the right boundary tube algebra
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}({\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
.

We can introduce a crossed product between
\mathbf{R}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
and
\mathbf{L}(_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D})
. It is noteworthy to emphasize the strong similarity with the concept of the quantum double of a given weak Hopf algebra
W
(see Definition
2
):
D(W)=(\hat{W}^{\rm cop}\otimes W)/J
, where the quantum double is derived from
W
and its dual
\hat{W}
through a crossed product.

(89)

Notice the crucial order here: if we take
\mathbf{R}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})\Join\mathbf{L}(_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D})
, the multiplication is inherited directly from the tube diagrams, obviating the necessity for additional F-move operations.
It is easy to check that for
X\in\mathbf{R}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
,
Y\in\mathbf{L}(_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D})
,
\Delta(X\Join Y)=\Delta(X)\Join\Delta(Y)
.
Using the natural embedding of the boundary tube algebras into the bulk tube algebra, the above construction implies that we can obtain the bulk tube algebra by taking crossed product of two boundary tube algebras
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})
and
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}({\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
.
To summarize, we have the following.

Proposition 11
.

The bulk tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
is isomorphic to the crossed product
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})\Join\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D})
.

Remark 4.5
.

Noticeably, we can also view
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})
as the dual of
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}({\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}})
, and vice versa, by embedding them into bulk diagrams. This will be illustrated in detail in Sec.
5
.

4.3
Topological excitation and representation of tube algebra

It is pertinent to remember that our tube algebra is derived from the trivial domain wall
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
. From the macroscopic theory of multifusion string-net, we know that the excitations associated with domain walls are defined by the category of
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule functors, denoted as
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
(it is braided monoidal equivalent to the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
).
The tensor product of two functors
F,G
is defined as
F\otimes G:=G\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}F
, namely, for
M\in{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
, we have
(F\otimes G)(M)=G\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}F(M)
.

For a bulk excitation
F\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
, we can construct a corresponding lattice model in the following way. We introduce the graded vector spaces

V_{F}:=\bigoplus_{x,y\in\operatorname{Irr}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})}\mathrm{Hom}_{{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}}(F(x),y),\quad V^{F}:=\bigoplus_{x,y\in\operatorname{Irr}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})}\mathrm{Hom}_{{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}}(x,F(y)).

(90)

(92)

We can introduce the vertex stabilizer
Q_{v_{9}}:V_{F}\to\tilde{V}_{F}
as a projector whose support space is the direct sum of the spaces such that
\mathrm{Hom}_{{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}}(F(x),y)\neq 0
, which we denote as
\tilde{V}_{F}
(a similar definition works for
\tilde{V}^{F}
). The face operators
B_{f_{L}},B_{f_{R}}
can be defined in a similar way as that for the bulk. Thus, we obtain the Hamiltonian:

H[\Sigma_{\rm ext},F]=-\sum_{i=1}^{9}Q_{v_{i}}-B_{f_{L}}-B_{f_{R}}.

(93)

It is clear that
V_{F}
and
V^{F}
form modules over the tube algebra, where the action is defined as in Eq. (
69
).
The tube algebra assumes the role of a local algebra, with the domain wall excitations serving as representations of this algebra.

4.4
Morita theory for the tube algebra

In this subsection, we denote the tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
as
\mathbf{T}^{0,0;0,0}
. The significance of the superscripts will be elucidated later. Building upon our earlier discussion, we observe that the topological excitations of the multifusion string-net model are delineated by the representation category of the tube algebra
\mathbf{T}^{0,0;0,0}
. It is noteworthy that
\mathbf{T}^{0,0;0,0}
represents the most basic tube obtained through local moves. This prompts an inquiry into the relationship between the algebras before and after these topological local moves.
The answer is that they are
Morita equivalent
.

Recall that two algebras
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
are called Morita equivalent if and only if their module categories
{}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathsf{Mod}
and
{}_{\mathcal{B}}\mathsf{Mod}
are equivalent.
It can be proved that
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
are
Morita equivalent if and only if there exist
\mathcal{A}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodule
M
and
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{A}
-bimodule
N
such that
M\otimes_{\mathcal{B}}N\cong\mathcal{A}
as
\mathcal{A}|\mathcal{A}
-bimodules and
N\otimes_{\mathcal{A}}M\cong\mathcal{B}
as
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules.

Let us consider the general tube space
\mathbf{T}^{m_{0},m_{1};n_{0},n_{1}}
spanned by the tube string-net configurations :

(95)

Note that we have omitted the morphism labels and object labels around the arcs for simplicity. For the gluing process to be meaningful, the number of internal edges in the first diagram must match the number of external edges in the second diagram. Hence, we set
m_{0}=m_{1}=m
and
n_{0}=n_{1}=n
to ensure compatibility. It is clear that this operation is associative by the diagrams. One can easily show that the unit is of the form

(97)

The right
\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}
-action on
\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}
is represented by stacking diagrams of
\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}
from inside of diagrams of
\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}
. Obviously these two actions are independent and hence endow the tube space
\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}
a bimodule structure.

To summarize, we have the following result:

Theorem 4
.

The tube space
\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}
are algebras for all
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
.
The tube space
\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}
forms a right-
\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}
and left-
\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}
bimodule.
These structures form a Morita context in the sense that

\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}\otimes_{\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}}\mathbf{T}^{s,m;t,n}\cong\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t},\quad\mathbf{T}^{s,m;t,n}\otimes_{\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}}\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}\cong\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}.

(98)

Thus
\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}
’s are Morita equivalent for all
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
.

Proof.

The first assertion has been shown, so it suffices to construct the isomorphisms. Define
\alpha:\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}\otimes_{\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}}\mathbf{T}^{s,m;t,n}\to\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}
by stacking the diagrams as in the definition of
\mu
in Eq. (
95
). This is a
\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}|\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}
-bimodule morphism. Define
\beta:\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}\to\mathbf{T}^{m,s;n,t}\otimes_{\mathbf{T}^{m,m;n,n}}\mathbf{T}^{s,m;t,n}
as follows:

Clearly
\beta
is also a
\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}|\mathbf{T}^{s,s;t,t}
-bimodule morphism. It is immediate that
\alpha\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\beta=\mathrm{id}
and
\beta\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}\alpha=\mathrm{id}
hold, thus the first isomorphism in Eq. (
98
) is proven. The second isomorphism can be demonstrated similarly.
∎

5
Gapped boundary theory

Gapped boundary conditions for the Levin-Wen string-net model can be established through various equivalent approaches
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Hu et al. 2018
;
Jia et al. 2023a
. Here, we will outline the application of the Kitaev-Kong construction to the multifusion string-net model. In this context, the gapped boundaries are characterized by module categories over the input UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
for some weak Hopf algebra
W
, which means that the bulk gauge weak Hopf symmetry is
W
.

It is crucial to highlight that, in contrast to the original Levin-Wen string-net model, even though the bulk phase is a UMTC, the ensuing boundary phase deviates from being a UFC. Instead, it assumes the structure of a UMFC, thereby introducing a notable distinction from the characteristics observed in the original model.

Definition 10
.

A gapped boundary phase is called stable if the boundary topological phase is a UFC. This inspires us to give the following two definitions:

1.

For a UMFC
\mathcal{D}
, a
\mathcal{D}
-module category
\mathcal{M}
is called stable if the functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M})
is a UFC.

2.

For a weak Hopf algebra
W
, a
W
-comodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
is called stable if the functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathsf{Rep}(W)}({{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod},{{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod})
is a UFC.

The lattice Hamiltonian of the gapped boundary
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}
can be formulated as follows. It is important to note that the boundary is oriented such that the bulk resides on the left-hand side of the boundary. For a boundary vertex
v_{b}
, it is connected to one bulk edge
e
and two boundary edges
e_{1}
and
e_{0}
:
e_{1}
ends at
v_{b}
, while
e_{0}
originates from
v_{b}
.
The bulk edge
e
is labeled with simple objects
j
in
\mathcal{D}
, but boundary edges
e_{1}
and
e_{0}
are labeled with simple objects
x_{1}
and
x_{0}
in
\mathcal{M}
.
We define
Q_{v_{b}}
as the projection operator such that, when applied to a boundary string-net configuration,
Q_{v_{b}}=1
if
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{M}}(j\otimes x_{1},x_{0})\neq 0
, and
Q_{v_{b}}=0
otherwise.
The boundary face operator
B^{k}_{f_{b}}
with
k\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
is defined as inserting a loop labeled by
k
in the boundary face
f_{b}
, and
B_{f_{b}}=\sum_{k}\frac{d_{k}}{\sum_{l}d_{l}^{2}}B^{k}_{f_{b}}
.
The boundary Hamiltonian is of the following form

H[\partial\Sigma,{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}]=-\sum_{v_{b}}Q_{v_{b}}-\sum_{f_{b}}B_{f_{b}}.

(99)

Notice that despite the similarity in expression to the bulk vertex and face operators, the boundary vertex and face operators are inherently distinct. When computing the matrix form of
B_{f_{b}}
, we require boundary topological local moves, which rely on the
\mathcal{D}
-module structure of
\mathcal{M}
. And in the definition of
Q_{v_{b}}
we need the fusion of bulk label and boundary label, which is also based on the
\mathcal{D}
-module structure of
\mathcal{M}
.
An intriguing observation is that any boundary model can be transformed into a UMFC string-net model. However, it is worth noting that the UMFC resulting from this transformation is larger than the original one, as will be discussed in Sec.
7
.

5.1
Boundary gauge symmetry

As previously discussed, the bulk gauge symmetry of the multifusion string-net model
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
is described by a weak Hopf algebra
W
such that
\mathsf{Rep}(W)\simeq\mathcal{D}
. An important question that arises is how to model the boundary gauge symmetry corresponding to the left
\mathcal{D}
-module category
\mathcal{M}
.
Here, we propose that the boundary gauge symmetry can be equivalently characterized by:

1.

W
-comodule algebra
\mathfrak{A}
. By definition, a left
W
-comodule algebra is a left
W
-comodule with left coaction
\beta_{\mathfrak{A}}:\mathfrak{A}\to W\otimes\mathfrak{A}
such that
\beta_{\mathfrak{A}}(xy)=\beta_{\mathfrak{A}}(x)\beta_{\mathfrak{A}}(y)
and
\beta_{\mathfrak{A}}(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=1_{W}\otimes 1_{\mathfrak{A}}
. A right
W
-comodule algebra can be defined similarly.

2.

W
-module algebra
\mathfrak{M}
. By definition, a left
W
-module algebra is a left
W
-module with left action
h\triangleright x
such that
h\triangleright(xy)=\sum_{(h)}(h^{(1)}\triangleright x)(h^{(2)}\triangleright y)
and
h\triangleright 1_{\mathfrak{M}}=\varepsilon(h)1_{\mathfrak{M}}
. A right
W
-module algebra can be defined similarly.

The equivalence between these two approaches is carefully discussed in our previous work
Jia et al. 2023a
.
Hereinafter, we will take the
W
-comodule algebra as a gapped boundary gauge symmetry.
For a given boundary gauge symmetry
\mathfrak{A}
, the module category
\mathcal{M}={{}_{\mathfrak{A}}}\mathsf{Mod}
is a module category over
\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Rep}(W)
.
The boundary excitations are characterized by
\mathcal{D}
-module functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M})
; via Eilenberg-Watts theorem, the boundary excitations can be equivalently characterized by the category
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathfrak{A}}^{W}
of
W
-equivariant
\mathfrak{A}|\mathfrak{A}
-bimodules.

Remark 5.2
.

\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{D}

\mathcal{D}
as a left
\mathcal{D}

{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})

Thus, we can perceive the bases of
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}})
and
\tilde{\mathbf{R}}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
as dual to each other.
This pairing is crucial for us to regard the bulk tube algebra as a quantum double, the details will be studied in our future work.

Remark 5.3
.

We can also introduce more bulk edges like that in Sec.
4.4
to construct the boundary tube space
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}^{m_{0},m_{1}}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}})
.
Different algebras
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}^{m,m}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}})

and
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}^{n,n}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}})
are Morita equivalent for
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
with Morita context given by bimodules
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}^{m,n}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}})
and
\tilde{\mathbf{L}}^{n,m}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}})
.

Remark 5.4
.

By leveraging the boundary-bulk duality, the boundary tube algebra can be viewed as the bulk gauge symmetry. Utilizing the boundary tube algebra as input data for the weak Hopf quantum double model yields a lattice model with identical topological excitations as those derived from the multifusion string-net bulk.

5.3
Anyon condensation

The gapped boundary phase can be regarded as a phase obtained from the bulk phase via anyon condensation
Bais et al. 2002
;
Bais et al. 2003
;
Bais and Slingerland 2009
;
Kong 2014
;
Eliëns 2010
;
Burnell 2018
.
There are at least three equivalent ways to understand bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation.

Shrinking approach.
—
For the multifusion string-net
\mathsf{SN}_{\mathcal{D}}
, the bulk excitations can be regarded as the defects over the domain wall
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
,
viz.
, we regarded
\mathcal{D}
as a
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule category.
The corresponding UMTC is given by
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
.
The topological phase of
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}
boundary is the left
\mathcal{D}
-module functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M})
. The anyon condensation can be regarded as a shrink of the region between the bulk
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
domain wall and
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}
boundary.
This shrinking process is achieved by the Deligne tensor product between module categories
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
and
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}
:
\mathcal{D}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}\simeq\mathcal{M}
.
A bulk excitation is a
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule functor
F:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}
; after anyon condensation, it becomes the functor
\mathcal{M}\simeq\mathcal{D}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}\overset{F\boxtimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{M}}}{\to}\mathcal{D}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}\simeq\mathcal{M}
, which is the same as anyon condensation of Levin-Wen string-net
Kitaev and Kong 2012
.

Lagrangian algebra approach.
—
Unlike the shrinking approach above and the tube algebra approach below, it is more convenient to distinguish the stable and unstable boundaries.
For the stable boundary, the bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation is described by the one-step anyon condensation theory
Kong 2014
;
Cong et al. 2017
;
Jia et al. 2022
;
Jia
, and there are two equivalent descriptions. The bulk phase is given by the UMTC
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
. The gapped boundary is determined by a Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
. The boundary phase is given by the category of
\mathcal{A}
-modules in
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})

12
12

12

For readers not familiar with tensor category theory, it is important to note that the concept of an
\mathcal{A}
-module here is distinct from the module over an algebra as typically defined in
\mathsf{Vect}
(the category of vector spaces).
An
\mathcal{A}
-module in
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
is an object
M\in\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
equipped with a morphism
\mu_{M}:\mathcal{A}\otimes M\to M
that satisfies the conditions:
\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mu_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{M})=\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mu_{M})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}a_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},M}
and
\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\eta_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{M})=l_{M}
, where
\eta:\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{A}
and
\mu_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
are structure morphisms of
\mathcal{A}
,
a_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},M}
is the associativity isomorphisms, and
l_{M}
is the left unit isomorphisms in
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
.
, which is usually denoted as
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})_{\mathcal{A}}
.
The Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}
also has a Frobenius algebra structure, from which we can construct a pre-quotient category
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})/\mathcal{A}
, then via taking Karoubi envelope, we obtain the boundary phase
\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D});\mathcal{A})
. It can be proved
Müger 2004
that
\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D});\mathcal{A})\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})_{\mathcal{A}}
, thus two descriptions are equivalent.

For the general case, including scenarios that are not necessarily stable, the bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation is described by a more intricate two-step condensation theory. In this part, we will provide an outline of the anyon condensation theory for multifusion string-nets. A more comprehensive discussion will be presented in
Jia
. It is worth recalling that the bulks we consider are always stable, i.e., their topological excitations are characterized by a unitary braided fusion category. The general multifusion phase will also be addressed in
Jia
.
Before we proceed to discuss the anyon condensation theory for multifusion topological phase, let us first introduce some necessary definitions.

Definition 11
.

A condensable algebra
\mathcal{A}
in a braided fusion category
\mathcal{P}
is an object
\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}
equipped with two structure morphisms: multiplication
\mu_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
and unit map
\eta_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{A}
, which satisfy

1.

(\mathcal{A},\mu_{\mathcal{A}},\eta_{\mathcal{A}})
is an algebra.

2.

\mathcal{A}
is commutative, i.e.,
\mu_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}c_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}}=\mu_{\mathcal{A}}
where
c_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}}
is the braiding map in
\mathcal{P}
.

3.

\mathcal{A}
is separable, i.e.,
\mu_{A}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
splits as a morphism of
\mathcal{A}|\mathcal{A}
-bimodules. Namely, there is an
\mathcal{A}|\mathcal{A}
-bimodule map
e_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{A}
such that
\mu_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}e_{\mathcal{A}}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

4.

\mathcal{A}
is connected, viz.,
\operatorname{dim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{1},\mathcal{A})=1
, the vacuum charge
\mathbf{1}
only appears once in the decomposition of
\mathcal{A}=\mathbf{1}\oplus a\oplus b\oplus\cdots
.

If an algebra satisfies conditions 1 and 2, it is referred to as an étale algebra
Davydov et al. 2013
. If a condensable algebra
\mathcal{A}
additionally satisfies
(\operatorname{dim}\mathcal{A})^{2}=\operatorname{dim}\mathcal{P}:=\sum_{a\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{P})}(d_{a})^{2}
, then
\mathcal{A}
is termed a Lagrangian algebra.

A left
\mathcal{A}
-module in
\mathcal{P}
is an object
M
equipped with a morphism
\mu_{M}:\mathcal{A}\otimes M\to M
such that,
\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mu_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{M})=\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mu_{M})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}a_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},M}
(where
a_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A},M}
is the associator in
\mathcal{P}
) and
\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\eta_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{M})=l_{M}
(where
l_{M}
is the left unit isomorphism in
\mathcal{P}
).
The right
\mathcal{A}
-module can be defined similarly.
For a commutative algebra, a left
\mathcal{A}
-module
M
is called local if and only if
\mu_{M}=\mu_{M}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}c_{M,\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}c_{\mathcal{A},M}
.

It can be proved that for Lagrangian algebra
\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}
, the category
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm loc}
of local
\mathcal{A}
-modules in
\mathcal{P}
is equivalent (as braided fusion category) to the category
\mathsf{Hilb}
of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces (corresponding to the trivial topological phase). And the category
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}
of
\mathcal{A}
-modules is a UFC.

To characterize the gapped boundary of multifusion string-net, we need extra data, an algebra
\mathcal{B}
in
\mathcal{P}
equipped with an algebra homomorphism
\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
. We say that
\mathcal{B}
is an algebra over
\mathcal{A}
if and only if

\mu_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{B}})=\mu_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\zeta_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}})\mathchoice{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.86108pt}{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}{\mathrel{\raisebox{0.43057pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$}}}c^{-1}_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}
.

With the above preparation, we are now ready to give our main result:

Theorem 5
.

For a multifusion string-net with bulk phase
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D})
, the bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation is characterized by a pair of algebras
(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
where
\mathcal{A}
is a Lagrangian algebra and
\mathcal{B}
is a separable algebra over
\mathcal{A}
. The boundary phase is characterized by the category
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}
of
\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}
-bimodules, which is a UMFC.
The bulk-to-boundary condensation is given by the monoidal functor

\bullet\otimes\mathcal{B}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}.

(107)

Proof.

Notice that the condensed phase is characterized by local
\mathcal{A}
-modules in
\mathcal{P}
. Since
\mathcal{A}
is a Lagrangian algebra, we have
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm loc}\simeq\mathsf{Hilb}
as unitary braided fusion categories. This implies that the condensed phase is a trivial topological phase. The boundary phase
\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{B}}
is a UMFC.
∎

Tube algebra approach.
—
Using the tube algebra description of the topological excitations that we have established before, we have another description of the bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation.
Since the bulk phase is given by the representation category of the bulk tube algebra
\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}))
, and the boundary phase is given by the representation category of the boundary tube algebra
\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}))
, the anyon condensation is a monoidal functor
\mathbf{Cond}:\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}))\to\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}))
.

Consider a disk region
\Gamma
in the bulk; if there are excitations inside this region, we examine the tube region
\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma}
surrounding this disk and construct the corresponding tube algebra. Anyon condensation can be viewed as enlarging the disk such that it can be treated as a boundary disk
\Gamma^{\prime}
.
For this boundary disk, we will have the corresponding boundary tube region
\operatorname{Tube}_{\Gamma^{\prime}}
, and through certain boundary topological local moves, we can derive the corresponding boundary tube algebra. In this manner, the bulk excitation transitions into a boundary excitation. See Fig.
4
for an illustration.

Figure 4:
Illustration of bulk-to-boundary anyon condensation based on tube algebra.

More precisely, let us consider a bulk excitation
M\in\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}))
, we denote its basis diagrammatically as

\begin{aligned} \hbox to20.62pt{\vbox to51.82pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 8.7359pt\lower-34.44322pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 23.62}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@fill@opacity{0.2}\lxSVG@begingroup@{fill-opacity} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -11.81 0 M -11.81 0 L -11.81 -23.62 L 11.81 -23.62 L 11.81 0 Z M 11.81 -23.62}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

\mathcal{D}
-module
\mathcal{M}
, the boundary vacuum is the identity functor
\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{M}}\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M})
. Using a construction similar to that given in subsection
4.3
, we obtain a
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})
-module
V_{\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{M}}}
, which represents the boundary vacuum charge. The basis consists of identity morphisms
\operatorname{id}_{m}
, where
m\in\mathcal{M}
.

where we have omitted the edge and vertex labels.
There is a natural action of
\mathbf{Tube}^{2;2}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})
on the basis elements given in Eq. (
109
), which means that we can map
bulk excitation
M\in\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}))
to boundary excitation
F_{1}(M)\in\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}^{2;2}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}))
with
F_{1}
denotes the corresponding functor.
Notice that
\mathbf{Tube}^{2;2}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})
is Morita equivalent to
\mathbf{Tube}^{0;0}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})=\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M})
; we denote the equivalence functor as
F_{2}:\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}^{2;2}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}))\to\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{M}))

The anyon condensation is thus described by
\mathbf{Cond}=F_{2}\circ F_{1}
.

Remark 5.5
.

Notice that Eq. (
70
) is the vertical fusion of two bulk excitations, where we need to use the comultiplication of the tube algebra. The vertical fusion corresponds to the composition
X\circ Y
of functors
X,Y\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
.
The anyon condensation we discussed above is indeed the horizontal fusion; it can also be generalized to the bulk topological excitations. Notice that in this case, the fusion corresponds to
X\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}Y
for
X,Y\in\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D})
.

6
Gapped domain wall theory

A gapped domain wall that separates two topological phases (UMTCs), denoted as
\mathcal{P}_{1}
and
\mathcal{P}_{2}
, can be converted into a gapped boundary of the stacked topological phase
\mathcal{P}_{1}\boxtimes\bar{\mathcal{P}}_{2}
. Here,
\bar{\mathcal{P}}_{2}
represents the phase obtained by applying the time-reversal transformation to
\mathcal{P}_{2}
. Mathematically, this transformation results in a UMTC with the same objects as
\mathcal{P}_{2}
but featuring anti-braiding structures.
This means that we can apply the result of gapped boundary in Sec.
5
to the gapped domain wall.
In this section, rather than adopting the aforementioned approach, we will delve into the domain wall tube algebra and domain wall excitations within the framework of the domain wall picture.
This viewpoint is valuable for advancing our understanding of gapped domain walls and gapped boundaries. It is noteworthy that gapped boundaries can be conceived as gapped domain walls that delineate a topological phase from a trivial or vacuum phase denoted as
\mathsf{Hilb}
.

For vertices
v_{w}
on the domain wall, we define the vertex operator
Q_{v_{w}}
in a similar way as that for the boundary (notice that the domain wall vertex is either for left
\mathcal{C}
-module structure over
\mathcal{M}
or for right
\mathcal{D}
-module structure over
\mathcal{M}
).
The face operator is also constructed by inserting loops inside the boundary faces.
The domain wall Hamiltonian is thus of the form

H[\Sigma_{1}\cap\Sigma_{2},{{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}}}]=-\sum_{v_{w}}Q_{v_{w}}-\sum_{f_{w,L}}B_{f_{w,L}}-\sum_{f_{w,R}}B_{f_{w,R}}.

(111)

If we set
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{D}
, we obtain the trivial
{{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}}
domain wall. It is observed that both the vertex operator and the two-sided face operators become identical to those for the
\mathcal{D}
bulk.

Remark 6.1
.

Consider two domain walls
{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}}
that separating multifusion string-nets with input UMFCs
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
, and
{}_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{E}}
that separating multifusion string-nets with input UMFCs
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{E}
, then two domain walls can fuse to obtain a new domain wall that separating multifusion string-nets with input UMFCs
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{E}
; this fusion process is mathematically characterized by the tensor product of module categories:
\mathcal{M}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{N}
.

A gapped domain wall
\mathcal{M}
is called invertible or transparent if it can be annihilated by its inverse domain wall
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
.
Mathematically, for the
\mathcal{C}|\mathcal{D}
-bimodule category
\mathcal{M}
, its opposite category
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
is a
\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{C}
-bimodule category;
\mathcal{M}
is called invertible if and only if there are equivalences
\mathcal{M}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}\simeq\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}\simeq\mathcal{D}
as bimodule categories
Etingof et al. 2010
.
The invertible domain walls are crucial because that the topological excitations can tunnel through the domain wall from one side to another.

6.1
Domain wall gauge symmetry

Consider two
2d
bulks of multifusion string-net with their respective UMFCs denoted as
\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}
. The associated weak Hopf gauge symmetries are represented by
W_{1}
and
W_{2}
for
\mathcal{D}_{1}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{1})
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}=\mathsf{Rep}(W_{2})
respectively. The gauge symmetry of the
1d
domain wall is characterized by the
W_{1}|W_{2}
-bicomodule algebra
\mathfrak{J}
, or equivalently by
W_{1}|W_{2}
-bimodule algebra
\mathfrak{K}
.

Assume the domain wall gauge symmetry to be
\mathfrak{J}
, then the module category
{}_{\mathfrak{J}}\mathsf{Mod}
over
\mathfrak{J}
is a
\mathcal{D}_{1}|\mathcal{D}_{2}
-bimodule category.
Thus the irreducible modules over
\mathfrak{J}
are labels of the domain wall string.

For two domain walls with gauge symmetry
\mathfrak{J}_{1}
and
\mathfrak{J}_{2}
respectively, the point defect between two domain walls are characterized by
\mathfrak{J}_{1}|\mathfrak{J}_{2}
-bimodules.
If
\mathfrak{J}_{1}=\mathfrak{J}_{2}=\mathfrak{J}
, these bimodules describe the topological excitations of the domain wall with gauge symmetry
\mathfrak{J}
.

(112)

Remark 6.2
.

When considering the defects between two domain walls
{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}}
and
{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{D}}
, we can construct a tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}[_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}};{{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{D}}}]
by setting the labels
f,g,h\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{M})
,
\zeta,\gamma\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{M}}
and
c,d,e\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{N})
,
\mu,\nu\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{N}}
.
It is clear that this forms an algebra, but there is no longer a coalgebra structure.
The defects between domain walls are thus characterized by the modules over
\mathbf{Tube}[_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{D}};{{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{D}}}]
.

(118)

The proof is the same as that for
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{D}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{D}})
.
∎

7
Defective string-net as a restricted multifusion string-net

In this section, we will elucidate a crucial application of the multifusion string-net model: a defective topological phase.
The main result is as follows:
Every defective string-net model is a restricted multifusion string-net model.
This implies that the multifusion string-net provides a general framework for investigating various defects of the
2d
topological phases.

7.1
Defective string-net from UMFC

Consider a
1d
surface with defects, including the
1d
domain wall or boundary and
0d
defects between different domain walls and boundaries.
Notice that all
1d
defects must have an orientation.
For an input UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
, we can label
2d
bulks with diagonal components
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
,
1d
defects with non-diagonal component
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
, the domain wall
0d
defects with
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}_{i,i}|\mathcal{D}_{j,j}}(\mathcal{D}_{i,j},\mathcal{D}_{i,j})
, and the boundary
0d
defects
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}_{i,i}}(\mathcal{D}_{i,j},\mathcal{D}_{i,j})
.
Since
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
is a
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}|\mathcal{D}_{j,j}
-bimodule category, and

\mathcal{D}_{i,j}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{D}_{j,j}}\mathcal{D}_{j,k}\simeq\mathcal{D}_{i,k},

(119)

using the fact that
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}|\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{N})=\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{N}
, we see that
0d
defects can also be labeled by objects in the UMFC.
For example, we have a well-defined labeling, e.g., as follows:

(120)

the
0d
defect is labeled by the functor category
\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{D}_{i,i}|\mathcal{D}_{j,j}}(\mathcal{D}_{i,j},\mathcal{D}_{i,j})
.
Similar to (
92
), we can introduce face operators and vertex operators in the vicinity of the defects.
We see that different bulks, domain walls and boundaries are labeled with different components of the input UMFC
\mathcal{D}
; this kind of model will be called a
restricted multifusion string-net
.
The above discussion implies that:
a restricted multifusion string-net gives a defective string-net
.
This can be summarized as follows:

Proposition 15
.

For a string-net model on a disk with boundary and boundary defects, the input data can be determined by a multifusion category
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
whose diagonal components
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
are UFCs that satisfy
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i,i})\simeq\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{j,j})
for all
i,j\in I
. And we have:

1.

The bulk input data is
\mathcal{D}_{0,0}
and the bulk topological phase is given by the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{0,0})
.

2.

The input data of type-
i
boundary is
\mathcal{D}_{0,i}
and the corresponding boundary excitation is characterized by
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
.

3.

The boundary defect between type-
i
and type-
j
boundaries (the
i|j
-boundary defects
13
13

13

Since there is a given orientation of the boundary, the
i|j
-defect is different from the
j|i
-defect.
) are described by
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
.

Notice that the space spanned by restricted string-net configurations is a subspace of the corresponding multifusion string-net, where there is no restriction of the string labels for different bulks and domain walls or boundaries, meaning that they all are chosen arbitrarily from
\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D})
.

For the reverse direction, we need to consider how to represent a given defective string-net as a restricted multifusion string-net.
This will be illustrated in the next subsection.

7.2
Example: defective Levin-Wen string-net as multifusion string-net

To understand why all defective string-net models can be regarded as restricted multifusion string-nets, let us consider the Levin-Wen string-net model as an example. We will demonstrate that
any defective Levin-Wen string-net can be naturally interpreted as a multifusion string-net
, as previously briefly outlined in Refs.
Kitaev and Kong 2012
;
Kong 2012
.
In the context of a defective Levin-Wen string-net, we will focus on boundaries and boundary defects, as illustrated in Fig.
5
. This formulation proves to be sufficiently general, as a domain wall can be seamlessly transformed into a boundary, and domain wall defects can be equivalently transformed into boundary defects.
We will take the disk as an example; the generalization to a more general case is straightforward.

Recall that, in the Kitaev-Kong construction, for a string-net model with the bulk UFC
\mathcal{C}
, the input data of the gapped boundary is an indecomposable
\mathcal{C}
-module category
\mathcal{M}

Kitaev and Kong 2012
.
In the construction of a string-net with a boundary, careful consideration is required for handling both the boundary data in the module category
\mathcal{M}
and the bulk data in
\mathcal{C}
. The labels for boundary edges are represented by simple objects denoted as
a\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{M})
, where no duality structure is inherently present.
To elucidate the meaning of
\bar{a}
, it is necessary to consider
\bar{a}
as an object in
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
, where
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
is the category that shares the same objects as
\mathcal{M}
but with reversed arrows. This prompts the question of how to define
b\otimes\bar{a}
and
\bar{a}\otimes b
.
It turns out that
b\otimes\bar{a}
can be regarded as an object in
\mathcal{C}
and
\bar{a}\otimes a
can be regarded as an object in
\mathcal{C}^{\vee}_{\mathcal{M}}:=\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M})

Kitaev and Kong 2012
.
The boundary defects (excitations) are characterized by the
\mathcal{C}
-module functors between
\mathcal{M}
and
\mathcal{M}
.
For string-net evaluations involving boundaries to be well-defined, we are tasked with embedding both
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{M}
into a multifusion category.

It is convenient to denote
\mathcal{M}_{0}=\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{M}_{1}=\mathcal{M}
, which are two left
\mathcal{C}
-module categories.
We can embed
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{M}
into a multifusion category denoted as
\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{def}}_{\mathcal{M}}:=\mathcal{C}_{0,0}\oplus\mathcal{C}_{0,1}\oplus\mathcal{C}_{1,0}\oplus\mathcal{C}_{1,1}
.
This expanded category can be understood as a direct sum of four components:

1.

UFC
\mathcal{C}_{0,0}:=\mathcal{C}
. Notice that we can regard
\mathcal{C}
as a category of
\mathcal{C}
-module functors since we have the equivalence
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})=\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{M}_{0},\mathcal{M}_{0})
.

2.

Left
\mathcal{C}
-module category
\mathcal{C}_{0,1}:=\mathcal{M}
.

3.

\mathcal{C}_{1,0}:=\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
(the opposite category of
\mathcal{M}
, which has the same objects as
\mathcal{M}
but with reversed morphisms).

4.

\mathcal{C}_{1,1}:=\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\vee}
, which encapsulates the category of
\mathcal{C}
-module functors mapping
\mathcal{M}
onto itself and inherently serves as a UFC.

The duality and fusion operation are closed for
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\vee}
. The dual object of
m\in\mathcal{M}
in
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm def}
can be regarded as
\bar{m}\in\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
which is the same object as
m
but all arrows are reversed.
Fusion between objects in
\mathcal{M}
and
\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
are defined as

m\otimes\bar{n}=\bigoplus_{i\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{C})}N_{in}^{m}i\in\mathcal{C}.

(121)

Fusion between
i\in\mathcal{C}
and
m\in\mathcal{M}
(resp.
\bar{n}\in\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
) is given by the left (resp. right)
\mathcal{C}
-module category structure:
i\otimes m\in\mathcal{M}
(resp.
\bar{n}\otimes i\in\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
).
We also need the fusion between
m\in\mathcal{M}
and
\tau\in\mathcal{C}^{\vee}_{\mathcal{M}}
: Since
\tau
is a
\mathcal{C}
-module functor from
\mathcal{M}
to itself, we have
m\otimes\tau=\tau(m)\in\mathcal{M}
. The last one is the fusion of
\bar{m}\in\mathcal{M}^{\rm op}
and
n\in\mathcal{M}
. We can define
\bar{m}\otimes n
as a
\mathcal{C}
-module functor by taking each
x\in\mathcal{M}
to
(x\otimes\bar{m})\otimes n
, thus
\bar{m}\otimes n\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\vee}
.
In summary, we have a multifusion category

\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{def}}_{\mathcal{M}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathcal{C}_{00}&\mathcal{C}_{01}\\
\mathcal{C}_{10}&\mathcal{C}_{11}\end{array}\right)

(122)

with fusion defined as

\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}x_{00}&x_{01}\\
x_{10}&x_{11}\end{array}\right)\otimes\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}y_{00}&y_{01}\\
y_{10}&y_{11}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}(x_{00}\otimes y_{00})\oplus(x_{01}\otimes y_{10})&(x_{00}\otimes y_{01})\oplus(x_{01}\otimes y_{11})\\
(x_{10}\otimes y_{00})\oplus(x_{11}\otimes y_{10})&(x_{10}\otimes y_{01})\oplus(x_{11}\otimes y_{11})\end{array}\right).

(123)

The tensor unit is
\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}\oplus\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\vee}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}&\\
&\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\vee}}\end{array}\right)
.
Now, we have all of the data we need:
\{N_{ab}^{c},\delta_{abc},d_{a},{N^{\prime}}_{am}^{n},\delta^{\prime}_{amn},d_{m}\}
, which determine the model.
Thus, to summarize, we see that a defective Levin-Wen string-net can be regarded as a multifusion string-net, for which the bulk is labeled by a diagonal component
\mathcal{C}_{0,0}
, the boundary is labeled by the category
\mathcal{C}_{0,1}
(or
\mathcal{C}_{1,0}
) which is in the same row (or column) as
\mathcal{C}_{0,0}
. The boundary defects are characterized by another diagonal component
\mathcal{C}_{1,1}
. The construction can be straightforwardly generalized to the case of
\Sigma=\Sigma_{g,l}
with
l
-different boundaries.

For a string-net model with bulk determined by a UFC
\mathcal{C}
, there are two types of defects: gapped boundaries (codimension 1) and boundary defects (codimension 2).
The gapped boundaries are classified by equivalence classes of
\mathcal{C}
-module categories
\mathcal{M}_{0},\cdots,\mathcal{M}_{n}
, where
\mathcal{M}_{0}=\mathcal{C}
is the smooth boundary and
\mathcal{M}_{n}=\mathsf{Vect}
is the rough boundary. Note that there exist smooth and rough boundaries for any string-net model.

Figure 5:
(a) A trivalent lattice in the vicinity of the boundary (bold arrows). (b) A disk with the bulk labeled by
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}=\mathcal{C}
and the boundary labeled by
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}=\mathcal{M}
.

The above observation can be generalized to the general case and we have the following result:

Proposition 16
.

Any defective Levin-Wen string-net model can be regarded as a restricted multifusion string-net.
For the Levin-Wen string-net model with bulk input UFC
\mathcal{C}
, the gapped boundaries are classified by equivalence classes of
\mathcal{C}
-module categories
\mathcal{M}_{0},\cdots,\mathcal{M}_{n}
, where
\mathcal{M}_{0}=\mathcal{C}
is the smooth boundary and
\mathcal{M}_{n}=\mathsf{Vect}
is the rough boundary. The defective Levin-Wen string-net can be regarded as a multifusion string-net with input UMFC as
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}_{0},\cdots,\mathcal{M}_{n}}^{\rm def}
, where
\mathcal{C}_{0,0}=\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathsf{Vect},\mathsf{Vect})
,
\mathcal{C}_{i,j}=\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{M}_{i},\mathcal{M}_{j})
.

Proof.

It is proved in Ref.
Etingof et al. 2005
that, for a given UFC
\mathcal{C}
and an indecomposable
\mathcal{C}
-module category
\mathcal{M}
, the category
\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{def}}_{\mathcal{M}}
is a unitary multifusion category.
∎

Remark 7.1
.

The above discussion also applies to the defective multifusion string-net model.

Conversely, given a UMFC, it is also possible to construct a defective Levin-Wen string-net as we have pointed out before.
Suppose that we have a UMFC
\mathcal{D}=\oplus_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
with
|\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{D}_{i,j})|=n_{i,j}
. Each diagonal component has a distinguished object
\mathbf{1}_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
, and we have
\mathbf{1}_{i}\otimes X_{i,j}\cong X_{i,j}
and
X_{i,j}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{j}\cong X_{i,j}
for all
X_{i,j}\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
. The tensor unit of
\mathcal{D}
is the direct sum of these objects
\mathbf{1}=\oplus_{i\in I}\mathbf{1}_{i}
.
The bulk’s input data can be chosen as an arbitrary diagonal component
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
.
The boundary input data now can be chosen as some component
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
which is a left
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
-module category. Since the dual object of
X_{i,j}\in\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
is
Y_{j,i}\in\mathcal{D}_{j,i}
, the complete data for the string-net model with a single boundary (i.e., on a disk) is the following sub-UMFC of
\mathcal{D}

\mathcal{D}[i;j]=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathcal{D}_{i,i}&\mathcal{D}_{i,j}\\
\mathcal{D}_{j,i}&\mathcal{D}_{j,j}\end{array}\right)

(124)

with fusion defined as

\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}X_{i,i}&X_{i,j}\\
X_{j,i}&X_{j,j}\end{array}\right)\otimes\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}Y_{i,i}&Y_{i,j}\\
Y_{j,i}&Y_{j,j}\end{array}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}(X_{i,i}\otimes Y_{i,i})\oplus(X_{i,j}\otimes Y_{j,i})&(X_{i,i}\otimes Y_{i,j})\oplus(X_{i,j}\otimes Y_{j,j})\\
(X_{j,i}\otimes Y_{i,i})\oplus(X_{j,j}\otimes Y_{j,i})&(X_{j,i}\otimes Y_{i,j})\oplus(X_{j,j}\otimes Y_{j,j})\end{array}\right).

Notice that for a fixed bulk
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
, the UMFC gives
|I|
different boundaries which are characterized by
\mathcal{D}[i,j]
with
j\in I
.
There always exists a special case that
\mathcal{D}[i;i]=\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
, called smooth boundary, where both the bulk and boundary are characterized by the UFC
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
.

Proposition 17
.

For a string-net with gapped boundary characterized by
\mathcal{D}[i;j]
, where the bulk label is taken from
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
, and the boundary label is taken from
\mathcal{D}_{i,j}
:

1.

The bulk phase is given by the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{D}_{i,i})
of
\mathcal{D}_{i,i}
.

2.

The boundary phase is given by the
\mathcal{D}_{j,j}
.

Proof.

This is evident from our previous discussion.
∎

8
Conclusion and discussion

In this work, we introduced the generalized multifusion string-net model and extensively discussed its macroscopic and microscopic properties.
Despite the progress that has been made, there remain several unresolved issues that warrant further investigation:

(i) A lattice realization of the correspondence between the multifusion string-net model and weak Hopf lattice gauge theory.
While for the Hopf case, the lattice realization of the equivalence is established in Refs.
Buerschaper and Aguado 2009
;
Buerschaper et al. 2013b
;
Jia et al. 2023a
, the problem for weak Hopf gauge symmetry largely remains open.

(ii) Applications in symmetry-enriched topological (SET) phases.
It has been noted in Ref.
Chang et al. 2015
that the multifusion string-net model provides a suitable framework for studying the SET phase.
A systematic and thorough investigation in this direction is still necessary.

(iii) The entanglement properties of the multifusion string-net are also of crucial importance. We know that the topological entanglement entropy is related to the quantum dimension of the topological excitations, and the entanglement entropy is sensitive to the defects of the model. Examining the entanglement features of the multifusion string-net model can provide us with deeper insights into its topological properties.

These problems will be the focus of investigation in our future endeavors.
